Rule: Speech may not be punished for stirring anger, inviting dispute, or creating unrest; it must pose a clear and present danger of a serious evil far above public inconvenience or annoyance.

Facts: A suspended priest's hate-filled speech to a packed auditorium risked violence with protesters outside. The jury was told "breach of the peace" included speech that "stirs the public to anger, invites dispute, brings about a condition of unrest, or creates a disturbance." Held: conviction reversed.

- Speech may best serve its purpose when it induces unrest or stirs people to anger; the alternative is standardized ideas.

- Dissent (Vinson, Frankfurter, Jackson, Burton): only that counsel failed to object to the instruction.

### Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969)

case · ch. 4Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969)

9-0 per curiam. Overruled Whitney v. California (1927).

Rule: Advocacy of force or law violation may be punished only if it is (1) directed to inciting or producing (2) imminent (3) lawless action and (4) is likely to produce it.

Facts: A KKK leader invited a reporter to film a farm rally: hooded figures, some armed, burned a cross; he warned of possible "revengeance" against the government and announced a march on Congress. Only Klan members and journalists were present. He was convicted under Ohio's criminal syndicalism law, which punished advocating violence and assembling to advocate it. Held: the statute is unconstitutional.

- Abstract teaching of the moral propriety or even necessity of force differs from "preparing a group for violent action and steeling it to such action."

- Ohio's law punished mere advocacy, with no intent, imminence, or likelihood requirement.

- Concurrences: Black and Douglas would expressly reject the "clear and present danger" test, which was used to affirm WWI dissidents' convictions (Abrams, Schaefer, Pierce). Douglas quotes Holmes in Gitlow: "Every idea is an incitement."

Era | Case(s) | Standard
1919-27 | Abrams, Schaefer, Pierce, Whitney | Clear and present danger / bad tendency used to punish dissident advocacy
1949-51 | Terminiello; Dennis | Clear and present danger of serious evil
1969-now | Brandenburg | Intent + imminence + likelihood (replaced the older test in practice)

### Fighting Words, Hostile Audiences, and Hate Speech

- Fighting words (Chaplinsky): personal insults so offensive they're likely to provoke the listener to attack the speaker immediately. The Court hasn't upheld a restriction on this theory since 1942. [Beyond casebook: Chaplinsky's facts — Walter Chaplinsky, a Jehovah's Witness distributing literature on a public street in Rochester, New Hampshire, called a city marshal "a God damned racketeer" and "a damned Fascist." The Court upheld his conviction under a state law against offensive words addressed to others in public.]

- Cohen v. California (1971): a "Fuck the Draft" jacket in a courthouse hallway was not fighting words — no one present could reasonably see a direct personal insult, and there was no realistic prospect of violence. (Profanity point in Ch. 6.)

- No heckler's veto (Cox v. Louisiana, 1965; Edwards v. South Carolina, 1963): peaceful civil rights protesters can't be convicted because a hostile crowd might become violent when police can control it.

- Police could control the crowd: in Cox, a hostile crowd of 100 to 300 was separated from the student protesters by 75 to 80 armed police; in Edwards, police protection "was at all times sufficient," and the City Manager admitted he could have brought more officers if needed.

- Hate speech is generally protected. In Collin (Ch. 3), the village conceded it expected no violence, taking the case outside both Brandenburg and Chaplinsky.

### R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, 505 U.S. 377 (1992)

case · ch. 4R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul (1992)

9-0 on the judgment, Scalia, J.

Rule: Government may ban an entire unprotected category because of what makes it proscribable, but it may not single out a subset based on topic or viewpoint.

Facts: Teenagers burned a cross in a Black family's fenced yard. St. Paul's ordinance banned symbols arousing anger "on the basis of race, color, creed, religion or gender," construed to reach only fighting words. Held: facially unconstitutional.

- Unprotected categories are not "invisible to the Constitution" — e.g., government may ban libel, but not only libel critical of the government.

- The ordinance was underinclusive: it didn't reach fighting words based on political affiliation, union membership, or sexual orientation.

Harvard note (1993, by coauthor Klein): Chaplinsky should be overruled rather than expanded — it rewards the undesirable response of fighting (unlike fleeing a false "Fire!") and gives police discretion to punish minorities and critics.

- The critique the note answers: scholars faulted Chaplinsky for assuming a white male "fight" response; women and outnumbered minorities may flee or submit instead. Prof. Kathleen Sullivan would extend the doctrine to words that cause "fright or flight" (otherwise there is "more license to insult Mother Teresa than Sean Penn"). The note's answer: abolish the doctrine rather than expand it.

### Prior Restraints and National Security

Prior restraint checklist. Is the government stopping speech before it occurs (an injunction or licensing), rather than punishing it afterward? If so, the restraint carries a heavy presumption of invalidity and the government bears a heavy burden. The only recognized exception is Near's wartime dictum (troop locations, transport sailing dates), which the Court has never actually applied.

### Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson, 283 U.S. 697 (1931)

case · ch. 4Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931)

Prior restraint on a newspaper.

Rule: A prior restraint on publication is presumptively unconstitutional. The protection "is not absolutely unlimited," but the limitation has been recognized "only in exceptional cases."

Facts: Under a state statute allowing "suppression of the offending newspaper or periodical," Minnesota courts enjoined The Saturday Press and its owner, J.M. Near, from continuing to publish articles that criticized local law enforcement as corrupt and inefficient. Held: reversed — the Framers especially opposed prior restraints. Dictum: protection isn't absolute; in wartime the government might prevent publication of troop numbers and locations or transport sailing dates.

### New York Times Co. v. United States, 403 U.S. 713 (1971) (Pentagon Papers)

case · ch. 4New York Times Co. v. United States (1971)

6-3 per curiam. Don't confuse with NYT v. Sullivan (defamation).

Rule: A prior restraint comes with a heavy presumption against validity (Bantam Books; Near); a general claim of harm to national security did not carry the government's heavy burden.

Facts: Daniel Ellsberg leaked a classified Vietnam War study showing the government knew the war likely couldn't be won and misled the public. The Nixon Administration sought to enjoin the Times and Post; publication was restrained for 15 days. Held: injunctions denied.

- Black (with Douglas): every moment of restraint was a flagrant violation; the press serves the governed, not the governors; "security" is a vague generality that can't override the First Amendment.

- Timeline: the Times published June 13, 1971; a temporary restraining order followed June 15; the Second Circuit enjoined the Times while the D.C. courts refused to enjoin the Post. The Court granted cert on June 25 (staying publication), heard argument June 26, and ruled June 30.

- Dissent (Burger, Harlan, Blackmun): the issues were hard and the decision too rushed.

- The briefs: the government argued a "real likelihood" of grave danger suffices and the President is best placed to judge it. The ACLU argued restraints should be limited to tactical military operations, weapons designs, and codes — and never for information bearing on public policy decisions. The government also argued that Near's examples were merely illustrative and that punishment after publication would be meaningless, since the harm would already be done. The ACLU's test had two parts: the information must fall in one of those narrow categories and must not bear on public debate. Even plans like the Bay of Pigs would stay protected (JFK later told the Times that more coverage "would have saved us from a colossal mistake"). It added that 12 of the 19 federal judges who had reviewed the papers rejected the government's harm claims.

- Why prior restraints are worse (Thomas Emerson, quoted by the ACLU): they bring a wider range of expression under scrutiny, shut off speech before it happens, are imposed "by a stroke of the pen" without the safeguards of criminal process, allow less public criticism, and drive toward excess.

- Aftermath: the Court has never upheld such a restraint. Marchetti and Snepp rested on CIA secrecy agreements (in Snepp the book's proceeds went to the government, and the Court never decided whether publication could be enjoined); The Progressive (H-bomb article) was enjoined but abandoned before appeal.

### Synthesis: Why Each Unprotected-Category Argument Failed

Case | Category | Why it failed
Terminiello | Incitement | Law reached speech that merely angered; no imminence
Brandenburg | Incitement | Punished mere advocacy; no intent, imminence, or likelihood
Cohen | Fighting words | No direct personal insult; no realistic violence
Cox, Edwards | Hostile audience | Police could control the crowd
Collin | Incitement; fighting words | Village conceded no expected violence
R.A.V. | Fighting words (assumed) | Banned only a topic-based subset
Near; Pentagon Papers | National security | Heavy presumption not overcome

### Stretch Exercise: The Courthouse Livestream

| Analysis
Facts | An activist livestreams outside a courthouse: "we need to shut this courthouse down today." Viewers push barricades; the activist adds, "I'm not telling anyone to hurt anybody. But history remembers people who act." Ten minutes later a group breaks through and damages the entrance.
Government | Imminence ("today," crowd at the target, ten minutes); a concrete call to action; urging escalation after seeing the pushing supports intent; likelihood shown by an agitated crowd already pressing forward.
Activist | Core criticism of government; "shut it down" is common, conditional protest rhetoric; explicit disclaimer of violence; much of the audience was online; punishing speakers for volatile listeners risks a heckler's-veto effect.
Likely answer | Close; turns on intent. The post-pushing statement is the government's best evidence, and a properly instructed jury could convict. [Beyond casebook: Hess v. Indiana (1973) and NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware (1982) support the activist on imminence and intent.]

## Chapter 5: True Threats and Speech Integral to Crime

Theme — mens rea as speech protection. The Court often forbids penalizing speech unless the speaker had a culpable mental state. This gives honest speakers "breathing room" at the cost of letting some unprotected speech go unpunished. Brandenburg requires intent; Counterman requires at least recklessness; Williams requires belief and intent.

### True Threats

### Counterman v. Colorado, 600 U.S. 66 (2023)

case · ch. 5Counterman v. Colorado (2023)

7-2 on the judgment, Kagan, J.

Rule: A true threat is a serious expression conveying that the speaker means to commit unlawful violence, judged by how a reasonable recipient would understand it. The First Amendment also requires proof that the speaker was at least reckless — consciously disregarding a substantial and unjustifiable risk that the words would be viewed as threatening.

Facts: Counterman sent hundreds of Facebook messages over two years to a musician he'd never met, creating new accounts when blocked; some suggested surveillance or harm ("Die."). She feared for her life and canceled performances. He was convicted under a stalking law applying a purely objective test. Held: vacated and remanded.

- "True" excludes jests and hyperbole ("I'll kill you if you leave dirty dishes in the sink").

- Why a subjective element: speakers unsure of the line, fearful of error or litigation costs, will self-censor protected speech.

- Why recklessness (not purpose or knowledge): it balances chilling against the real harms of threats; reckless speakers consciously accept a substantial risk of serious harm.

- The statute: Colorado's stalking law barred repeated communications made "in a manner that would cause a reasonable person to suffer serious emotional distress" and that did so; the only evidence was his messages.

- Barrett's guardrails: true threats are already narrow. The speaker must express an intent to commit unlawful violence against a particular person or group, judged by a reasonable listener who knows the whole context (tone, audience, medium, the broader exchange). Sotomayor added that online speech lacks contextual clues and that racial and cultural stereotypes can shape what a jury sees as dangerous.

Opinion | Standard | Core reason
Majority (Kagan, Roberts, Alito, Kavanaugh, Jackson) | Recklessness | Balances chilling against harm to victims
Concurrence (Sotomayor; Gorsuch in part) | Intent | Online speech lacks context; juries' norms and stereotypes vary; incitement (the closest cousin) requires intent
Dissent (Barrett, Thomas) | Objective only | Other categories use objective tests; the category is already narrow and context-sensitive; let legislatures calibrate

### Speech Integral to Crime

Unprotected whether written or spoken: speech that is the crime ("Your money or your life"), offers or solicits illegal acts ("I'll sell you heroin"; "I want to hire a prostitute"), or helps commit or conceal one ("I'll tell you when the coast is clear" — conspiracy, aiding and abetting). Abstract advocacy of illegality ("cocaine should be legal") stays protected. Hard cases: general-audience how-to material (novels are protected; bomb manuals?).

### United States v. Williams, 553 U.S. 285 (2008)

case · ch. 5United States v. Williams (2008)

7-2, Scalia, J.

Rule: Offers to provide and requests to obtain contraband are categorically unprotected (Giboney; Pittsburgh Press). A law is void for vagueness only if it fails to give fair notice or invites seriously discriminatory enforcement — not merely because close cases exist.

Facts: A federal law criminalized pandering or soliciting child pornography — offers or requests concerning material the defendant believes (or intends another to believe) is child pornography. Held: constitutional and not vague.

- Solicitation, conspiracy, and incitement laws have always criminalized speech intended to induce crime; such offers have no social value.

- "Promotes" doesn't reach "child pornography should be legal" or even "I encourage you to obtain it"; it means recommending a particular item with intent to initiate a transfer (distinguishing abstract advocacy — Brandenburg; Claiborne Hardware).

- Vagueness comes from the Due Process Clause. It concerns indeterminacy about what fact must be proved ("annoying," "indecent"), not difficulty proving it; that is handled by the reasonable-doubt standard. Belief and intent are true-or-false facts.

- Vagueness standard: a law is void if it fails to give a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited, or is so standardless that it invites seriously discriminatory enforcement. In First Amendment cases the Court relaxes the rule that someone whose own conduct is clearly covered can't complain of vagueness as to others. Still, "perfect clarity" has never been required.

- Dissent (Souter, Ginsburg): statute-specific; no dispute that speech integral to crime is unprotected.

| Vagueness | Overbreadth
Complaint | Law is unclear | Law reaches too much protected speech
Source | Due Process | First Amendment
Whose speech | Mainly the litigant's own (Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project — casebook says "Rights") | Third parties' (Stevens, Hansen)
Shared goal | Prevent chilling | Prevent chilling

### Rice v. Paladin Enterprises, Inc., 128 F.3d 233 (4th Cir. 1997)

case · ch. 5Rice v. Paladin Enterprises, Inc. (1997)

3-0, Luttig, J.

Rule: Speech — even publishing — that aids and abets a crime is unprotected where the publisher intended to assist criminals and the material was used exactly as intended.

Facts: Paladin published Hit Man, a detailed manual for contract killers; Perry used it to murder three people. Paladin stipulated that it intended to assist murderers and knew the book would be used "upon receipt" for murder. Held: the First Amendment doesn't bar the victims' families' aiding-and-abetting suit.

- Copycat cases differ: readers misuse novels and films; publishers don't intend to assist crime.

- Evidence of intent will almost never exist apart from stipulations like these.

- News reporting is never a basis for liability.

- Not all manuals: the stipulations, detailed instructions, exhortation to murder, and lack of any legitimate purpose made the case unique.

- More stipulations: Perry also followed another Paladin book, How to Make a Disposable Silencer, and Paladin stipulated that it assisted Perry in these very murders. Major networks, newspapers, and publishers filed as amici warning that "no expression" would be safe; the court said copycat cases involve misuse, not use "precisely as intended."

### Stretch Exercise: A Bomb Manual Without Stipulations

| Analysis
For prosecution | Aiding and abetting is speech integral to crime; publishers aren't exempt (Paladin); operational know-how, not ideas; catastrophic harm.
Against | No extrinsic intent evidence; legitimate audiences (engineers, researchers, journalists, novelists); general publication isn't a one-to-one offer like Williams; Stevens bars creating categories by balancing.
What the government should prove | Specific intent to facilitate a crime (as in Brandenburg, not Counterman's recklessness), evidence beyond the text itself, actual use in a crime, and narrow construction (Hansen). [Beyond casebook: 18 U.S.C. § 842(p) takes this intent-based approach.]

### Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)

case · ch. 5Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc. (2025)

Conway, J. Preliminary ruling.

Rule: A distributor may assert its users' right to receive speech, but output counts as speech only if it is expressive; the court was not prepared to hold that chatbot output is speech.

Facts: In the first wrongful-death suit against an AI chatbot company, a 14-year-old (Sewell Setzer III; the casebook spells it "Seltzer") died by suicide after heavy use of Character.AI. The complaint alleges an anthropomorphized, manipulative design marketed to children. Held (preliminary): First Amendment dismissal denied.

- Relying on Barrett's Moody v. NetChoice concurrence: an algorithm carrying out a human's expressive choice may be speech; when owners "hand the reins" to an LLM, it's unclear any person made an expressive choice.

- Why the companies relied on users' rights: claiming the output as the company's own expression would mean owning its words and the liability for them, would admit deliberate design (like Paladin's stipulations, helping prove intent), and would reinforce the product-design framing. [Beyond casebook: it would also undercut Section 230 immunity for third-party content.]

- The allegations: chatbot characters sent romantic messages and urged him to stay "loyal"; when he expressed suicidal thoughts, the system steered back to the subject instead of activating safeguards; he died immediately after a character told him to "come home." The company allegedly worked in partnership with Google.

- Weak analogies: the defendants compared the characters to non-player characters in video games and to other users on social media, both of which get First Amendment protection, but the court found they "do not meaningfully advance" those analogies.

Casebook study tips. Learn case names as shorthand for doctrines: "under Chaplinsky," "the Brandenburg rule," "Giboney and its progeny," "under Counterman." Know the most recent case on each doctrine, since the Court refines and sometimes overrules its earlier cases. In practice, cite binding precedent: your circuit and the Supreme Court in federal court, or the state's high and appellate courts in state court. Other decisions are only persuasive authority. Failing to cite binding precedent can be a professional-responsibility violation.

## Chapter 6: Immoral Speech

Categories: obscenity, sexually explicit speech, child pornography, profanity, and violent imagery. "Indecent" describes speech regarded as immoral but not obscene. What unites them: the government seeks to suppress the speech for reasons of morality.

Immoral speech checklist. (1) Did the Court treat the speech as an unprotected category (rational basis only)? (2) If disputed, how did it define the category's boundaries (e.g., Miller; "obscene for kids")? (3) If protected, what standard of review applied (content-based usually means strict scrutiny)? (4) What was the bottom line, and why? Then ask the two overarching questions: Who is the government protecting, adults or kids? And what harm is targeted, harm from the content itself or an indirect harm, such as exploitation of real children?

### Governing Principles

- Adults: the government almost never can restrict immoral speech to protect adults from its content. The exception is obscenity, narrowly defined. Offended adults are expected to look away, walk away, or toss out the mail.

- Kids: the government sometimes can protect kids, especially from sexually explicit speech — but it can't block adult access, and kids have their own First Amendment rights (Brown).

- Secondary effects: local governments may zone adult businesses to reduce crime and lower property values (Renton).

- Child pornography made with actual children may be banned to dry up the market for abuse (Ferber) — not virtual images or adult look-alikes (Free Speech Coalition). But offers to buy or sell material believed to involve real children may be punished (Williams).

### Who Are We Protecting: Adults or Kids?

### Bolger v. Youngs Drug Products Corp., 463 U.S. 60 (1983)

case · ch. 6Bolger v. Youngs Drug Products Corp. (1983)

9-0 on the bottom line, Marshall, J.

Rule: The government can't shield adults from immoral content (except obscenity). It can shield kids from some content, but only if the restriction doesn't stop adults from getting it. The government "may not reduce the adult population to reading only what is fit for children."

Facts: A federal law banned mailing unsolicited contraceptive ads to homes. Held: the ban violates the First Amendment.

- Shielding adults from offense "carries little weight." Outside obscenity, offensiveness doesn't justify suppression; recipients aren't a captive audience, and "the short, though regular, journey from mail box to trash can is an acceptable burden" (citing Cohen).

- Helping parents is "undoubtedly substantial," but the ban fails: parents already control their mail, and the ban purges material "entirely suitable for adults."

- Butler v. Michigan: such a ban would "burn the house to roast the pig"; mailbox discourse can't be limited to "that which would be suitable for a sandbox."

- Pacifica distinguished as narrow: broadcasting is "uniquely pervasive" and "uniquely accessible to children."

### Cohen v. California, 403 U.S. 15 (1971)

case · ch. 6Cohen v. California (1971)

5-4, Harlan, J. (Fighting-words point in Ch. 4.)

Rule: The presence of unwilling viewers doesn't automatically justify suppressing offensive speech; they can "avoid further bombardment of their sensibilities simply by averting their eyes."

Facts: Cohen wore a jacket reading "Fuck the Draft" in a Los Angeles courthouse corridor where women and children were present, to show the depth of his feelings about the Vietnam War. He was convicted of disturbing the peace by offensive conduct (30 days). Held: reversed; the speech was protected.

### FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726 (1978)

case · ch. 6FCC v. Pacifica Foundation (1978)

5-4 on the bottom line; Stevens, J., plurality.

Rule: The government may regulate a broadcast that is indecent but not obscene, because broadcasting is uniquely accessible to children. The holding is narrow and rests on a nuisance rationale in which context is all-important.

Facts: A radio station aired George Carlin's "Filthy Words" monologue at 2 p.m. A father driving with his young son complained. The FCC issued a declaratory order finding the broadcast indecent, without formal sanctions. Held: the FCC's action was upheld.

- Why broadcasting is special: children have access to radios, often unsupervised; radios are in the home, where privacy gets extra deference; unconsenting adults may tune in without warning; and spectrum is scarce and licensed in the public interest.

- The FCC's approach: it found authority in 18 U.S.C. § 1464 ("obscene, indecent, or profane language" by radio) and used a nuisance model that channels rather than bans. A valuable broadcast preceded by warnings might be acceptable late at night but not when children are listening. Pacifica had warned listeners and aired the monologue during a program on attitudes toward language.

- Cohen's written message might have been incomprehensible to a first grader, but the broadcast "could have enlarged a child's vocabulary in an instant."

- Nuisance: time of day, program content, and medium matter. A nuisance may be "a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard."

- Not decided: two-way radio, an occasional expletive, or criminal prosecution. Pacifica returns in Ch. 9 (time, place, and manner).

Takeaway from Cohen and Pacifica: profanity is protected speech. Calling speech "indecent" or "profane" generally doesn't mean it can be restricted (Cohen; the FCANCER plate, Ch. 4, a district court case). Pacifica is the unusual, narrow exception.

### Protecting Adults: Obscenity and Secondary Effects

Rule: Obscenity is unprotected. Under Miller v. California (1973), still good law, speech is obscene only if all three are met: (a) the average person, applying contemporary community standards, would find the work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest; (b) it depicts or describes, in a patently offensive way, sexual conduct specifically defined by state law; and (c) the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

Miller v. California facts: [Beyond casebook; the casebook states the test, quoted in Hudnut, but doesn't excerpt the case.] Marvin Miller ran a mass-mailing campaign advertising "adult" books and a film. His unsolicited brochures, with explicit pictures, were opened by a restaurant manager and his mother in Newport Beach, California, who complained to the police. He was convicted under California's obscenity law. Held: vacated and remanded under the new three-part test, which replaced the earlier "utterly without redeeming social value" standard and allowed local, rather than national, community standards.

- The challenge: defining obscenity without sweeping in valuable sexually explicit works. Before Miller, Justice Stewart said, "I know it when I see it" (Jacobellis, 1964), and the Court's "movie days" gave lower courts little guidance. Justices Black and Douglas skipped the movie days because they thought obscenity is protected speech (Bob Woodward, The Brethren).

- Prurient interest means "a shameful or morbid interest in nudity, sex, or excretion," not a normal interest in sex (Brockett v. Spokane Arcades, 1985).

- Prong (c) matters most: it protects works that, as a whole, have value, even if isolated scenes might seem obscene.

- Because obscenity is defined so narrowly, much deeply offensive speech is protected — and the casebook agrees it's more dangerous to let government go down that path.

- Some Justices continued to dissent that the Miller test is imprecise and chills protected speech, but it remains good law, with no serious chance of being overruled.

Hudnut revisited (full case in Ch. 3): the Indianapolis ordinance didn't track Miller — no prurient interest, no offensiveness, no community standards, no work-as-a-whole inquiry, and value was irrelevant. Its drafters saw those omissions as virtues; the court saw viewpoint discrimination. Drafter Catharine MacKinnon asked, "if a woman is subjected, why should it matter that the work has other value?"

### Renton v. Playtime Theatres, Inc., 475 U.S. 41 (1986) — Secondary Effects

case · ch. 6Renton v. Playtime Theatres, Inc. (1986)

Described in the casebook.

Rule: Zoning laws that confine adult businesses get intermediate scrutiny, even though partly content-based, because they target secondary effects (crime, property values), not the message.

Facts: The casebook describes the setting generally: cities use zoning to keep adult establishments, such as strip clubs and adult bookstores, out of residential and mainstream commercial areas, often concentrating them in one area. [Beyond casebook: Renton, Washington, barred adult movie theaters within 1,000 feet of any residential zone, dwelling, church, or park, and within one mile of any school. Playtime Theatres bought two theaters to show adult films and challenged the ordinance. The Court noted that more than 520 acres, over 5% of the city, stayed open to adult theaters.] Held: upheld under intermediate scrutiny, because the ordinance aimed at secondary effects (higher crime, lower property values) rather than the message.

The doctrine is narrow: the Court has refused to extend it beyond adult entertainment establishments.

### Protecting Kids: Child Pornography

### New York v. Ferber, 458 U.S. 747 (1982)

case · ch. 6New York v. Ferber (1982)

Unanimous on the bottom line, White, J.

Rule: Child pornography made with real children is unprotected, even if not obscene under Miller, because distribution is intrinsically related to the sexual abuse of the children used to make it.

Facts: New York criminalized distributing material depicting sexual performances by children under 16, without requiring obscenity. Held: upheld.

- Preventing sexual exploitation and abuse of children is an objective of "surpassing importance."

- Ferber was the Court's first look at a statute limited to sexual depictions of children. The federal government and 47 states had laws aimed at production, and at least half of them didn't require obscenity; Miller had been an accommodation between protecting unwilling recipients and the dangers of censorship.

- Two links to abuse: the materials are a permanent record, and circulation worsens the harm; and the distribution network must be closed to control production.

- Production is clandestine, but marketing needs a visible apparatus, so drying up the market may be the only practical method of enforcement.

- The value of such material is "exceedingly modest, if not de minimis."

- Casebook note: the rationale resembles secondary effects — the harm is indirect (abuse of real children in production), not caused by the message.

### Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition, 535 U.S. 234 (2002)

case · ch. 6Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002)

6-3, Kennedy, J. Thomas concurred in the judgment; O'Connor concurred in part and dissented in part; Rehnquist and Scalia dissented.

Rule: Ferber does not extend to sexually explicit images made without real children (computer-generated images or adults who look like minors).

Facts: The Child Pornography Prevention Act of 1996 (CPPA) banned sexually explicit images that "appear to" depict minors. Held: the extension violates the First Amendment.

- It goes beyond Ferber, whose rationale depended on protecting real children exploited in production.

- It bans speech regardless of serious value. Teen sexuality and child abuse are enduring themes in art — Juliet is 13 in Romeo and Juliet.

- "Appear to be under 18" is higher than many states' ages for marriage and consent.

- One explicit scene would trigger punishment without inquiry into value, but "the artistic merit of a work does not depend on the presence of a single explicit scene."

- Ferber itself relied on virtual images as a permissible alternative; the CPPA criminalized that alternative.

United States v. Williams revisited (Ch. 5): offers and requests for child pornography are speech integral to crime. The tricky part: the law covered material the buyer or seller believed depicted a real child. The Court held such offers may be punished even if the belief is mistaken, stressing that technology makes it nearly impossible to prove which images involve real children.

### Protecting Kids: Age-Gating

### Ashcroft v. ACLU, 542 U.S. 656 (2004) ("Ashcroft II")

case · ch. 6Ashcroft v. ACLU (2004)

5-4, Kennedy, J. Rehnquist, O'Connor, Scalia, and Breyer dissented.

Rule: Under strict scrutiny, a content-based law that suppresses a large amount of speech adults have a right to receive is invalid if less restrictive alternatives would be at least as effective; the government must prove they are not.

Facts: The Child Online Protection Act (COPA) criminalized posting material "harmful to minors" online for commercial purposes, with an affirmative defense for age verification (e.g., a credit card). Held: likely unconstitutional.

- Filters are less restrictive: they restrict at the receiving end, not the source; adults needn't identify themselves; and no speech is criminalized, so chilling is diminished.

- Filters may be more effective: they block foreign sites, can't be evaded by minors with credit cards, and cover email.

- Filters are imperfect, but the government offered no specific evidence that COPA would work better.

### Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, 145 S. Ct. 2291 (2025)

case · ch. 6Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025)

6-3, Thomas, J. Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson dissented.

Rule: A law requiring age verification to keep minors from speech that is obscene as to them gets intermediate scrutiny, because its burden on adults is incidental. Texas's law satisfies it.

Facts: Texas H.B. 1181 requires commercial websites publishing sexually explicit content to verify visitors' ages. Held: constitutional.

- Two traditional powers: states may ban speech obscene to the public at large, and may prevent children from accessing speech that is obscene to children (the Miller test adjusted for minors; Ginsberg v. New York, 1968). Ginsberg upheld a ban on selling minors sexual material that would be obscene from a child's perspective.

- Why intermediate scrutiny: any burden on adults is "only an incidental effect on protected speech" (Boy Scouts v. Dale).

- Earlier cases distinguished: Reno v. ACLU (1997) applied strict scrutiny because the Communications Decency Act operated as a ban on adult speech; its age-verification defense was illusory given the technology. The internet has changed dramatically since Reno and Ashcroft II (smartphones, streaming).

- Rational basis rejected: it applies only when no fundamental rights are implicated; adults have a real, if incidentally burdened, right. Intermediate scrutiny is "deferential but not toothless."

- The test: a law survives intermediate scrutiny if it advances important governmental interests unrelated to the suppression of free speech and does not burden substantially more speech than necessary. Texas and the Fifth Circuit had argued for rational basis.

- Applied: the interest in shielding children from sexual content is "important, even compelling." The law adapts traditional in-person age checks to the digital age, using government ID or transactional data — methods used for online gambling, alcohol, tobacco, car rentals, and by the pornography industry itself. Less restrictive alternatives (filters, ISP blocking) don't defeat a legitimate legislative choice under intermediate scrutiny. Privacy is protected by the incentives of sites and verifiers, and stigma has never exempted the industry from regulation.

Question to consider: did Paxton effectively overrule Ashcroft II? The filtering alternative that won in 2004 lost in 2025 because of the lower standard of review. The Court framed the earlier cases as involving effective bans on adult access.

### Protecting Kids: Violent Imagery

### Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, 564 U.S. 786 (2011)

case · ch. 6Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011)

7-2, Scalia, J. Alito (with Roberts) concurred; Thomas and Breyer dissented.

Rule: Violent imagery is protected; there is no new unprotected category for violence, even for minors. A content-based ban on selling violent video games to minors gets strict scrutiny, and California's fails.

Facts: California banned selling or renting "violent video games" to minors. Held: unconstitutional.

- Video games are speech: they communicate ideas through characters, dialogue, plot, music, and interaction; it is "difficult to distinguish politics from entertainment, and dangerous to try."

- No new category (following Stevens): legislatures can't add categories by balancing value against social costs — a "startling and dangerous" proposition. Obscenity covers only depictions of sexual conduct, not violence.

- Ginsberg distinguished: it adjusted an existing category (obscenity) for minors; California sought a wholly new category for children only.

- Minors' rights: minors are entitled to a significant measure of First Amendment protection; there is no "free-floating power to restrict the ideas to which children may be exposed."

- No tradition: Grimm's fairy tales, the Odyssey, Dante's Inferno, and Lord of the Flies are full of gore. Past panics targeted dime novels, movies, radio, comics, television, and music.

- Interactivity isn't new (choose-your-own-adventure books); it differs in degree, not kind. Judge Posner: all literature is interactive.

- Strict scrutiny fails: no causation (the research shows correlation, suffers methodological flaws, and finds minuscule effects); wildly underinclusive (similar effects from Bugs Bunny cartoons, E-rated games, even pictures of guns), which alone defeats the law; and the industry's rating system already helps parents, so filling the "modest gap" isn't compelling.

- The evidence: California conceded it couldn't show a direct causal link. Its main expert, Dr. Craig Anderson, relied on studies that every court to consider them had rejected; he admitted the effects were "about the same" as those of violence on television.

### Synthesis: Standards and Outcomes

Case | Speech | Protecting | Standard | Result
Cohen (1971) | Profanity | Adults | Protected | Conviction reversed
Pacifica (1978) | Indecent broadcast | Kids | Narrow broadcast / nuisance rationale | FCC upheld
Bolger (1983) | Contraceptive ads | Adults and kids | Protected; interests insufficient | Ban struck
Miller (1973) | Obscenity | Adults | Unprotected (three-part test) | Test defined
Hudnut (1985) | "Degrading" explicit material | Adults | Viewpoint discrimination | Struck
Renton (1986) | Adult business zoning | Communities | Intermediate (secondary effects) | Upheld
Ferber (1982) | Child porn with real children | Real children | Unprotected | Upheld
Free Speech Coalition (2002) | Virtual child porn | Kids | Protected | Struck
Williams (2008) | Offers and requests for child porn | Real children | Speech integral to crime | Upheld
Ashcroft II (2004) | Online material harmful to minors | Kids | Strict | Struck (filters)
Paxton (2025) | Online age verification | Kids | Intermediate | Upheld
Brown (2011) | Violent video games | Kids | Strict | Struck

### Stretch Exercise: Teen Sexting

| Analysis
Issue | Should consensual teen sexting be treated as unprotected child pornography? Such images often fit statutory definitions; some states reduce penalties for teens, many don't, federal law draws no distinction, and prosecutors have discretion.
Questions | Does Ferber's rationale (drying up a market that exploits children) fit a 15-year-old sending her own image to a partner? If not, may the government regulate it at all? Should the partner's age matter (15, 17, 18, 25)? What if a 15-year-old partner forwards the image to others ("revenge porn")?
Analysis | Ferber's market-and-exploitation rationale fits poorly for a self-made image shared consensually with a peer. Its other harm — a permanent record whose circulation worsens the injury — fits forwarding well. A sensible rule would turn on exploitation: an adult partner or nonconsensual redistribution looks like Ferber; consensual exchange between peers does not.

## Chapter 7: Torts Involving Speech

Big picture: state law defines the elements of a tort, but when speech is an element, especially the central one, the First Amendment limits how a state may define it. The Court's rules are a compromise: let victims of speech-based torts recover in some circumstances without chilling too much protected speech, especially criticism of government officials. Torts covered: fraud, defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED), invasion of privacy, and appropriation of likeness or intellectual property.

Speech-tort checklist. (1) Is the question about Torts, the First Amendment overlay, or both (bar tip)? (2) Who is the plaintiff: public official, public figure, or private person? (3) Is the speech on a matter of public or private concern? (4) What mens rea does the First Amendment require (knowledge, recklessness/"actual malice," negligence)? (5) What damages are sought: actual, presumed, or punitive? (6) For true information: was it obtained lawfully, and is it of public concern? The same conduct can be both a tort and a crime; the First Amendment principles are typically the same.

### Fraud

Rule: Fraud is an unprotected category of speech. Common law requires (1) a false statement of material fact, (2) made knowing it was false, (3) with intent to mislead, usually to obtain money or property. Those demanding mens rea elements greatly reduce the risk of chilling protected speech.

- Why unprotected: (1) history: fraud has been unprotected since 1791 (the Alvarez list); (2) the demanding common-law elements. A mere false statement is not enough.

- Hansen (Ch. 3) is fraud: he sold a sham "adult adoption" path to citizenship for $4,500 each, luring 450+ noncitizens and nearly $2 million. "The First Amendment does not shield fraud."

- Alvarez (Ch. 3) is not fraud: his lie about the Medal of Honor was "a pathetic attempt to gain respect," not made to secure employment or financial benefits.

### Defamation

Defamation is a traditional tort for injury to reputation. Libel is written; slander is spoken ("s" for spoken). Before 1964 the First Amendment put no limits on it: the plaintiff showed the defendant said something bad about him, truth was a defense the defendant had to prove, and damages were presumed. The First Amendment rules now vary along two axes: (a) is the plaintiff a public official/public figure or an ordinary person, and (b) is the statement on a matter of public or private concern?

Four questions to answer from the cases. (1) Why protect false statements of fact at all? (2) Why make it harder for public officials and public figures to sue? (3) Why make it harder when the statement involves a matter of public concern? (4) Are the lines convincing?

### New York Times v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964)

case · ch. 7New York Times v. Sullivan (1964)

9-0 on the bottom line, Brennan, J. Black, Douglas, and Goldberg would have given absolute immunity to critics of public officials.

Rule: A public official can't recover damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves "actual malice": the statement was made "with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." Recklessness is enough; "malice" here does not mean ill will.

Facts: In 1960 the Times ran a full-page ad by supporters of Martin Luther King Jr. criticizing Montgomery, Alabama police's treatment of civil rights protesters. It had factual errors (how many times King had been arrested, which song protesters sang). Police commissioner L. B. Sullivan sued and won $500,000 under Alabama's easy-to-prove libel law. Held: reversed.

- Breathing space: "erroneous statement is inevitable in free debate," and it must be protected if freedom of expression is to have the "breathing space" it needs to survive.

- Truth defense isn't enough: requiring critics to guarantee the truth of every assertion, on pain of unlimited judgments, leads to self-censorship. Critics would "steer far wider of the unlawful zone," even when what they say is true, out of doubt it can be proved or fear of the expense.

- The press: the rule is especially important to the press, which roots out and reports on corrupt or inefficient officials, but the press gets no greater First Amendment rights than individuals.

- Don't confuse this New York Times case with the Pentagon Papers case (Ch. 4).

### Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts, 388 U.S. 130 (1967)

case · ch. 7Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts (1967)

Plurality. Described in the casebook commentary and slides; not excerpted.

Rule: The Sullivan actual-malice standard extends to public figures, not just public officials.

Facts: A magazine accused Wally Butts, former University of Georgia football coach, of conspiring with Alabama's coach to fix games. Butts couldn't recover without showing actual malice.

### Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., 418 U.S. 323 (1974)

case · ch. 7Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974)

5-4, Powell, J. Burger, Douglas, Brennan, and White dissented.

Rule: When a private person sues over a statement on a matter of public concern, states may set their own standard of liability so long as they don't impose liability without fault (at least negligence). But presumed or punitive damages require actual malice.

Facts: The casebook omits the complicated facts. The key point: the plaintiff was an ordinary private person, but the false statement involved an issue of public concern.

- "No such thing as a false idea": opinions are corrected by competing ideas, not judges and juries. But false statements of fact have no constitutional value; "neither the intentional lie nor the careless error" advances debate.

- Strategic protection: because error is inevitable and strict liability causes "intolerable self-censorship," the First Amendment "requires that we protect some falsehood in order to protect speech that matters."

- Why private plaintiffs get more protection: (1) self-help: public officials and figures have greater access to the media to rebut lies, so private people are more vulnerable; (2) normative: public officials and figures voluntarily exposed themselves to scrutiny; a private person "has relinquished no part of his interest in the protection of his own good name," so he is more deserving of recovery.

- Public figures: some are public figures for all purposes (persuasive power and influence); more commonly, people become public figures by thrusting themselves to the forefront of particular public controversies. Truly involuntary public figures are "exceedingly rare."

- Damages: juries' "largely uncontrolled discretion" to award presumed or punitive damages where there is no loss compounds the chilling effect.

### Dun & Bradstreet, Inc. v. Greenmoss Builders, Inc., 472 U.S. 749 (1985)

case · ch. 7Dun & Bradstreet, Inc. v. Greenmoss Builders, Inc. (1985)

5-4; Powell, J., plurality (with O'Connor and Rehnquist). Burger and White concurred in the judgment; Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, and Stevens dissented.

Rule: When a private plaintiff sues over a statement on a matter of purely private concern, presumed and punitive damages may be awarded without actual malice. Open question, still undecided 40 years later: may a state impose strict liability, or does the First Amendment require at least negligence?

Facts: A credit reporting company issued false credit reports about a construction contractor to the contractor's creditors. Held: presumed and punitive damages allowed.

- Balancing: the state's interest in compensating private reputational injury is the same as in Gertz, but the First Amendment interest is weaker. Speech on matters of public concern is at the heart of the First Amendment; purely private speech poses no threat to debate on self-government and no risk of press self-censorship. It is "not totally unprotected," but its protections are less stringent.

- White, J., concurring in the judgment: he had joined Sullivan but came to think it struck an "improvident balance." Under it "the lie will stand": the defeated official gets no judgment identifying the falsehood, and the public stays misinformed. He would have kept the common-law liability standard and instead capped damages, so a defamed official could at least get a judgment vindicating his reputation.

### Berisha v. Lawson, 141 S. Ct. 2424 (2021) (denying cert.)

case · ch. 7Berisha v. Lawson (2021)

Gorsuch, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari (Thomas, J., also dissented separately).

Point: Sullivan's actual-malice standard remains good law, and there is no sign a majority wants to revisit it. But Justices Thomas and Gorsuch have urged the Court to reconsider it.

- Founding view: freedom of the press meant no prior restraints, not freedom to defame without consequence. Publishers had a duty to try to get the facts right or answer in tort, the accepted view for over two centuries until 1964.

- Changed media landscape: in 1964 a handful of large, fact-checked print and broadcast outlets dominated; today virtually anyone can publish virtually anything instantly. Disinformation is cheap and profitable, while the economic model supporting reporters and fact-checkers has eroded.

- What began as tolerating occasional falsehood has become "an ironclad subsidy for the publication of falsehoods by means and on a scale previously unimaginable."

- Discussion prompt: would you keep, replace, or abolish the actual-malice standard? The casebook points to President Trump's $20 billion defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal over statements linking him to Jeffrey Epstein.

### Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress

IIED is a relatively new, more controversial tort that not all states recognize. It typically requires that the defendant intentionally or recklessly caused the plaintiff severe emotional distress through extreme and outrageous conduct. The Court has extended its defamation principles to IIED claims based on speech.

### Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, 485 U.S. 46 (1988)

case · ch. 7Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (1988)

8-0, Rehnquist, C.J. (Kennedy, J., recused).

Rule: Public figures and public officials may not recover for IIED based on a publication unless it contains a false statement of fact made with actual malice. "Outrageousness" is too subjective a standard to satisfy the First Amendment.

Facts: Hustler ran a parody ad portraying Jerry Falwell, a nationally known minister and political commentator, in a drunken incestuous encounter with his mother in an outhouse. Falwell won an IIED verdict. Held: reversed. The ad was obviously a parody and couldn't reasonably be read as stating actual facts.

- Otherwise, political cartoonists and satirists would face damages without any showing that their work falsely defamed its subject.

- The ad was "at best a distant cousin" of political cartoons, but there is no principled standard to separate them. "Outrageousness" has "an inherent subjectiveness" that lets juries impose liability based on their tastes, views, or dislike of the expression.

### Snyder v. Phelps, 562 U.S. 443 (2011)

case · ch. 7Snyder v. Phelps (2011)

8-1, Roberts, C.J. Alito, J., dissented.

Rule: Speech on a matter of public concern, in a public place, is entitled to "special protection" and can't be the basis for IIED liability just because a jury finds it outrageous. The focus is the content of the speech (public concern), not the plaintiff's identity (here, a private person).

Facts: Fred Phelps and Westboro Baptist Church members picketed near the funeral of a soldier killed in Iraq, with signs saying God kills American soldiers to punish the nation's tolerance of homosexuality. The soldier's father won millions on an IIED claim. Held: reversed.

- Public concern: judged by all the circumstances. The signs addressed the political and moral conduct of the United States, homosexuality in the military, and Catholic clergy scandals, even if they fell "short of refined social or political commentary."

- Where and how: they picketed peacefully on public land next to a public street, about 1,000 feet away and out of sight of the church, under police supervision, with no shouting, profanity, or violence, and didn't disrupt the funeral. The distress came from the content and viewpoint of the message: parishioners holding "God Bless America" signs at the same spot wouldn't have been liable.

- "If there is a bedrock principle," the government may not prohibit an idea because society finds it offensive. In public debate we must tolerate "insulting, and even outrageous, speech" to give the First Amendment "breathing space."

### Counterman Revisited: Borrowing From Defamation

Counterman v. Colorado (2023) (full case in Ch. 5) held that a true-threats prosecution requires at least recklessness as to whether the communication would be seen as threatening. Justice Kagan borrowed directly from Sullivan and Gertz: a subjective mental-state requirement is "strategic protection" against the chilling effect. It shields some proscribable speech, but by reducing an honest speaker's fear of accidental liability it gives "breathing room" to valuable speech. The First Amendment "requires that we protect some falsehood in order to protect speech that matters."

### Disclosing Information That Is True

Rule: Truthful information is protected speech. The Court is quite protective of disclosures, at least where the speaker obtained the information lawfully.

- Florida Star v. B.J.F. (1989), 6-3: a damages award against a newspaper for publishing a rape victim's name violated the First Amendment. The paper got the name lawfully from a publicly released police report. Applying strict scrutiny, the state lacked a compelling interest in preventing disclosure in those circumstances.

- Bartnicki v. Vopper (2001), 6-3: a media organization couldn't be held liable for broadcasting a tape of phone calls that a third party had illegally intercepted. Privacy is important but was outweighed by the right to publish truthful information on a matter of public concern.

- Revenge porn (state courts): the Supreme Court hasn't decided it. In Nebraska v. Zitterkopf (Neb. 2024), the defendant secretly recorded a sexual encounter and shared an image. Applying strict scrutiny, the court upheld the law: the state has a compelling interest in personal privacy, and the law is narrowly tailored even without an intent-to-harass element, because the harm from distributing intimate images is the same whatever the motive.

### Appropriation of Likeness or Intellectual Property

IP law is complicated and not covered in depth. Know only that federal and state laws can significantly protect intellectual property without violating the First Amendment, though there are limits.

### Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co., 433 U.S. 562 (1977)

case · ch. 7Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. (1977)

5-4, White, J. Powell, Brennan, Marshall, and Stevens dissented.

Rule: The First Amendment does not immunize the media from a state right-of-publicity claim when they broadcast a performer's entire act without consent.

Facts: Hugo Zacchini performed a 15-second "human cannonball" act at an Ohio county fair. He asked a freelance reporter not to film it; the next day, on the producer's instructions, the reporter taped the entire act, which aired on the 11 o'clock news with favorable commentary. Held: Zacchini's damages suit may proceed.

- Earlier cases involved reporting on events, not broadcasting an entire act a performer is normally paid for. It is like broadcasting a copyrighted play, a prize fight, or a ball game without permission.

- Broadcasting the whole act threatens its economic value. Like patent and copyright, the right of publicity gives an incentive to invest in a performance. Zacchini didn't seek to stop the broadcast; "he simply wants to be paid for it."

- Ohio may choose to privilege the press here, but the First Amendment doesn't require it.

### Synthesis: Defamation and IIED Rules

Plaintiff / speech | Case | Liability standard | Presumed / punitive damages
Public official | NYT v. Sullivan (1964) | Actual malice | Actual malice
Public figure | Curtis Publishing v. Butts (1967) | Actual malice | Actual malice
Private person, public concern | Gertz (1974) | At least negligence (no liability without fault) | Actual malice required
Private person, private concern | Dun & Bradstreet (1985) (plurality) | Open: negligence or strict liability? | No actual malice needed
IIED, public figure/official | Hustler v. Falwell (1988) | False statement of fact + actual malice | Same
IIED, speech on public concern in public place | Snyder v. Phelps (2011) | "Outrageousness" not enough | Same

### Stretch Exercise: The AI Campaign Video

| Analysis
Issue | A mayor vetoes a living-wage ordinance. Her opponent's campaign ad uses AI to create a realistic video of her saying, "I do not care whether working families can afford rent," with a small caption: "Dramatization based on the mayor's living-wage veto." Many viewers miss the caption and think it's real. She sues for defamation.
Questions | Is the video a statement of fact, opinion, parody, or something in between? Does the disclaimer matter? Does the political context make the speech more protected or more harmful? How does actual malice apply when the defendant knowingly fabricated the image but believed it captured the "truth" of the veto?
Analysis | The mayor is a public official and the speech concerns her official conduct, so Sullivan requires actual malice. Unlike Hustler's obviously absurd parody, a realistic video can reasonably be understood as stating an actual fact (that she said those words), and an easily missed disclaimer may not change that. The defendant knew the quotation was fabricated, which points toward knowledge of falsity, though he will argue the gist (her veto) was true and the video was rhetorical characterization. The political context cuts both ways: it is core speech that needs breathing space, but fabricated quotations in a campaign are the falsehoods Gertz says have no constitutional value.

## Chapter 8: Commercial Speech

What it is: speech used to try to sell stuff (goods or services): iPhones, sneakers, a haircut, legal services. Speakers are typically for-profit businesses, but nonprofits can engage in it (a nonprofit hospital advertising its specialty services). Charitable solicitations (fundraising) are not commercial speech. Because of the money involved, commercial speech is litigated far more often than obscenity or true threats.

Big picture: the Court lets governments restrict commercial speech more easily than other speech (Central Hudson, intermediate scrutiny), and compel commercial disclosures more easily still (Zauderer). That's why drug packaging carries health warnings and food carries nutrition labels.

Commercial speech checklist. (1) Is it commercial speech? (2) Is the government restricting speech or compelling a disclosure? (3) Restriction: run Central Hudson. Is the speech misleading or about illegal activity (unprotected)? If protected: substantial interest? directly advances? not more extensive than necessary? Watch for paternalism toward adults (fails) versus kids (may work, if tailored). (4) Compelled disclosure: run Zauderer. Purely factual and uncontroversial information about the seller's own product or service? reasonably related to a substantial interest? not unjustified or unduly burdensome? If Zauderer doesn't apply (NIFLA), use heightened scrutiny.

### Restrictions on Commercial Speech

### Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, 425 U.S. 748 (1976)

case · ch. 8Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council (1976)

8-1, Blackmun, J. Rehnquist, J., dissented.

Rule: For the first time, commercial speech is protected by the First Amendment. A state may not completely suppress truthful information about entirely lawful activity because it fears the information's effect on speakers and listeners. Commercial speech can still be regulated (false or misleading ads, illegal transactions, time/place/manner rules).

Facts: Virginia made it "unprofessional conduct," punishable by fines and loss of license, for a pharmacist to advertise prescription drug prices. A resident who took daily prescription drugs and two nonprofits challenged the law. Held: unconstitutional.

- Listeners have rights: where a willing speaker exists, protection extends to the communication, its source, and its recipients. "If there is a right to advertise, there is a reciprocal right to receive the advertising."

- Why protect it: the consumer's interest in commercial information "may be as keen, if not keener by far," than in the day's political debate. The ban hit hardest the poor, the sick, and the aged. Society needs intelligent, well-informed private economic decisions in a free-enterprise economy.

- Anti-paternalism: Virginia feared price competition would drive out "professional" pharmacists. The alternative is to assume "people will perceive their own best interests if only they are well enough informed" and to open channels of communication. Virginia may set professional standards but not by "keeping the public in ignorance."

- Footnote 24, why commercial speech gets less protection: it is more easily verifiable (the advertiser knows its own product) and more durable (advertising is the sine qua non of profits, so it is unlikely to be chilled). So there is less need to tolerate inaccuracy, warnings and disclaimers may be required, and the prior-restraint bar may not apply.

### Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission of New York, 447 U.S. 557 (1980)

case · ch. 8Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission of New York (1980)

8-1 on the bottom line, Powell, J. Brennan, Blackmun, and Stevens concurred in the judgment; Rehnquist, J., dissented.

Rule (the Central Hudson test, still good law): (1) Commercial speech is unprotected if it is misleading or concerns unlawful activity. If protected, ask: (2) Is the government's interest substantial? (3) Does the regulation directly advance that interest (not "ineffective or remote support")? (4) Is it not more extensive than necessary? Prongs 2-4 are a form of intermediate scrutiny.

Facts: New York completely banned promotional advertising by electric utilities to conserve energy. Held: the ban violates the First Amendment.

- The First Amendment's concern for commercial speech rests on the informational function of advertising, so the government may ban messages more likely to deceive than inform, or tied to illegal activity.

- Applied: the speech wasn't inaccurate or unlawful; energy conservation is plainly substantial; but the record failed to show a total ban was no more extensive than necessary.

### 44 Liquormart, Inc. v. Rhode Island, 517 U.S. 484 (1996)

case · ch. 844 Liquormart, Inc. v. Rhode Island (1996)

Unanimous on the bottom line; splintered opinions. Stevens, J., plurality (reasoning later adopted by the full Court).

Rule: Paternalism toward adults is not a valid reason to suppress truthful, non-misleading commercial speech. Blanket bans on such speech about lawful products get "special care" and rarely survive. If the government wants to reduce adult consumption, it must regulate the product directly (ban it, regulate prices, or tax it).

Facts: Rhode Island banned advertising the retail prices of alcoholic beverages to promote temperance. Held: invalid.

- Such bans rest on "the offensive assumption that the public will respond 'irrationally' to the truth." Be "especially skeptical of regulations that seek to keep people in the dark for what the government perceives to be their own good."

- Prong 4 fails: higher prices could be maintained by direct regulation or increased taxation (the state's own expert conceded this), so there was no "reasonable fit."

- No "greater includes the lesser": the power to ban alcohol doesn't include the power to ban ads for it. The Constitution presumes regulating speech is more dangerous than regulating conduct.

### Sorrell v. IMS Health Inc., 564 U.S. 552 (2011)

case · ch. 8Sorrell v. IMS Health Inc. (2011)

6-3, Kennedy, J. Breyer, Ginsburg, and Kagan dissented.

Rule: A law imposing content- and speaker-based burdens on commercial speech is subject to heightened scrutiny. The fear that people will make bad decisions if given truthful information can't justify it, even more so when the audience is sophisticated (doctors). "That the State finds expression too persuasive does not permit it to quiet the speech."

Facts: Vermont barred the sale and use of pharmacy records revealing individual doctors' prescribing practices for marketing, and barred drug makers from using them for "detailing" (sales visits to doctors). Vermont wanted to cut costs and steer doctors toward cheaper, safer generics. Held: unconstitutional.

- Content- and speaker-based: the law disfavored marketing (particular content) and drug manufacturers (particular speakers), while many other speakers could use the same information.

- The dissent argued the law regulated conduct (data mining), not speech; the casebook sets that issue aside.

### Lorillard Tobacco Co. v. Reilly, 533 U.S. 525 (2001)

case · ch. 8Lorillard Tobacco Co. v. Reilly (2001)

5-4 in relevant part, O'Connor, J. Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer dissented.

Rule: Some paternalism toward kids is allowed: the government may restrict accurate commercial speech to discourage minors' consumption, but the restriction must still satisfy Central Hudson prongs 3 and 4. If it keeps too much truthful information from adults, it fails prong 4.

Facts: Massachusetts banned outdoor tobacco ads within 1,000 feet of a school or playground, and indoor point-of-sale ads lower than 5 feet from the floor in stores within that radius. Held: both fail.

- Interest: preventing underage tobacco use is substantial, "and even compelling," and there was evidence that limiting youth exposure to ads reduces underage use.

- Outdoor ban fails prong 4: it would cover 87%-91% of Boston, Worcester, and Springfield, included in-store ads visible from outside, applied to ads of any size, and even reached oral statements. In some areas it was nearly a complete ban on truthful information to adults, who have a right to receive it (Bolger: mailbox discourse can't be limited to what suits "a sandbox").

- 5-foot rule fails prongs 3 and 4: "Not all children are less than 5 feet tall, and those who are certainly have the ability to look up."

### Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc., 515 U.S. 618 (1995)

case · ch. 8Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc. (1995)

5-4, O'Connor, J. Kennedy, Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg dissented.

Rule: A 30-day ban on targeted direct-mail solicitation of accident victims and their families by personal injury lawyers survives Central Hudson. It is the rare attorney-advertising restriction the Court has upheld.

Facts: Florida Bar rules barred personal injury lawyers from sending targeted direct mail to victims and relatives for 30 days after an accident or disaster. Held: upheld.

- Background: Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (1977) struck a ban on price ads for "routine" legal services; lawyer advertising is commercial speech with a measure of protection, and most restrictions have been struck.

- Substantial interest: protecting the privacy and tranquility of victims and their loved ones against intrusive contact, and the profession's reputation.

- Directly advances: the Bar's 106-page summary of a two-year study, with statistical and anecdotal data, showed the public views post-accident mail as intrusive and reflecting poorly on lawyers.

- Tailoring: the ban is brief, and lawyers can still use TV, radio, newspapers, billboards, and untargeted letters.

- The casebook's guess: the Justices were squeamish about "ambulance chasing" tarnishing the profession.

### Compelled Commercial Speech

Compelled commercial speech means the government requires sellers to say something about their products or services, usually in ads or on packaging: "contains peanuts," drug side effects, "contains small parts," or that a "free trial" auto-renews. These are often called disclosure requirements. Zauderer gives governments much more latitude to compel disclosures than to restrict truthful commercial speech.

### Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, 471 U.S. 626 (1985)

case · ch. 8Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel (1985)

Unanimous in relevant part, White, J.

Rule (the Zauderer test): The government may require purely factual and uncontroversial information about the terms under which the seller's services are available if the requirement is reasonably related to a substantial government interest (here, preventing consumer deception) and is not unjustified or unduly burdensome.

Facts: Philip Zauderer's ads said he handled cases on contingency and "if there is no recovery, no legal fees are owed by our clients." Ohio required disclosure that clients might still owe costs. Held: the Court struck Ohio's restrictions on attorney ads but upheld the disclosure requirement.

- Disclosure is not prohibition: Ohio didn't stop attorneys from conveying information; it only required "somewhat more information."

- Not Barnette or Wooley: Ohio didn't prescribe orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or opinion, only factual terms of commercial service.

- Why more lenient: commercial speech is protected mainly for its value to consumers (Virginia Pharmacy), so the advertiser's interest in not providing factual information is "minimal." Disclosure requirements "trench much more narrowly" on advertisers than flat bans.

- Applied: laypeople don't know "fees" and "costs" differ, so the ad suggested a no-lose proposition. No factual basis showed the requirement was unduly burdensome.

### Milavetz, Gallop & Milavetz v. United States, 559 U.S. 229 (2010)

case · ch. 8Milavetz, Gallop & Milavetz v. United States (2010)

9-0 on the bottom line, Sotomayor, J.

Rule: Zauderer, not Central Hudson, governs factual disclosures aimed at inherently misleading commercial ads.

Facts: Federal bankruptcy law (§ 528) required "debt relief agencies," including attorneys who help file bankruptcy petitions, to identify themselves as such in ads, with related disclosures. Milavetz preferred to be called a law firm. Held: upheld.

- Shares Zauderer's features: it combats ads promising debt relief without mentioning bankruptcy and its costs; it requires only an accurate statement of legal status and services; and it doesn't stop the advertiser from saying more.

- The "confusing label" claim fails: no evidence it confuses; it is accurate by definition; the required "helps people file for bankruptcy relief" gives context; the firm can add that it is a law firm; and it may tailor wording if substantially similar.

### National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA), 585 U.S. 755 (2018)

case · ch. 8National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra (2018)

5-4, Thomas, J. Breyer, Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan dissented.

Rule: Zauderer does not apply to a required notice that is not about the speaker's own services or that addresses a controversial topic. Even where Zauderer applies, a disclosure fails if it is unjustified (purely hypothetical harm) or unduly burdensome (drowns out the speaker's message).

Facts: California's FACT Act required (1) licensed clinics serving pregnant women to post notice that the state provides free or low-cost services, including abortion, with a phone number; and (2) unlicensed clinics to state they are not licensed medical facilities. The targets were "crisis pregnancy centers," largely faith-based pro-life organizations. Held: both requirements violate the First Amendment.

- Licensed notice: Zauderer doesn't apply. The notice in no way relates to the clinics' own services, and abortion is "anything but an 'uncontroversial' topic." It fails even intermediate scrutiny: it is wildly underinclusive (most of nearly 1,000 community clinics serving 5.6 million patients are exempt), and the state could run its own public-information campaign. It "cannot co-opt the licensed facilities to deliver its message."

- Unlicensed notice: fails even under Zauderer. Its justification was "purely hypothetical" (practicing medicine without a license is already a crime). It is unduly burdensome: a government-scripted notice on all print and digital ads, in larger or contrasting type, in as many languages as the state chooses. It "drowns out the facility's own message."

- The Court did not question "health and safety warnings long considered permissible" or purely factual disclosures about commercial products.

- Slides: the licensed notice failed because it was (1) not about services the clinics offered and (2) controversial (steering patients toward abortion). Professor Klein's guess: (1) alone would have been enough.

### CTIA - The Wireless Ass'n v. City of Berkeley, 928 F.3d 832 (9th Cir. 2019)

case · ch. 8CTIA - The Wireless Ass'n v. City of Berkeley (2019)

2-1, W. Fletcher, J. (court of appeals case). Friedland, J., dissented, finding the disclosure confusing.

Rule: Zauderer isn't limited to preventing deception. Any substantial interest, including public health and safety, can support a factual, uncontroversial disclosure.

Facts: Berkeley required cell phone retailers to give buyers a notice that federal radio-frequency (RF) exposure guidelines exist "to assure safety," that carrying an ON phone in a pocket or bra may exceed them, and to consult the user manual. It could be an 8.5 x 11 poster or a 5 x 8 handout bearing the city's logo; retailers could add their own clearly separate information. Held: upheld.

- Other circuits agree: country-of-origin labels on meat (American Meat Institute, D.C. Cir. en banc 2014); mercury labeling (NEMA v. Sorrell, 2d Cir. 2001); cigarette health warnings (Discount Tobacco, 6th Cir. 2012). NIFLA signaled agreement by preserving health and safety warnings.

- Two NIFLA limits on "factual and uncontroversial": (1) the notice can't take sides in a heated political controversy at odds with the speaker's mission; (2) it must relate to the speaker's own product or service.

- Applied: health and safety is substantial; the notice summarizes what the FCC already requires manufacturers to tell users. It is "largely reassuring," not inflammatory. Not unduly burdensome, unlike San Francisco's soda warning that had to fill 20% of each ad (American Beverage, 9th Cir. en banc 2019).

### Unpacking the Zauderer Test (Slides)

Element | What it means
Factual and uncontroversial | The Supreme Court has said little. Courts of appeals say a disclosure can qualify even if the seller dislikes it ("drinking alcohol while pregnant can cause birth defects"). NIFLA: must concern the seller's own services and not take sides in a controversy.
Substantial interest | Preventing consumer deception surely counts (Zauderer, Milavetz). Courts of appeals also accept health and safety ("contains peanuts," "nicotine is addictive") and things consumers care about, like country of origin ("Made in China"). Satisfying "idle consumer curiosity" probably isn't enough.
Reasonably related | Undefined by the Court. Less demanding than Central Hudson prong 4. Some circuits treat it as rational basis; Professor Klein's guess: more demanding than rational basis but still quite deferential.
Unjustified or unduly burdensome | "Unjustified" overlaps with reasonable relation. "Unduly burdensome" means the requirement chills commercial speech; courts say a disclosure that drowns out the seller's own message is unduly burdensome, which in practice restricts the speech.

### Synthesis: Restrictions vs. Compelled Disclosures

Case | Regulation | Result and reason
Virginia Pharmacy (1976) | Ban on drug price ads | Struck; commercial speech is protected; anti-paternalism
Central Hudson (1980) | Ban on utility promotional ads | Struck; total ban more extensive than necessary
Florida Bar (1995) | 30-day ban on targeted lawyer mail | Upheld; study evidence, brief ban, many alternatives
44 Liquormart (1996) | Ban on liquor price ads | Struck; paternalism toward adults; tax or regulate instead
Lorillard (2001) | Outdoor and 5-foot tobacco ad rules | Struck; too much burden on adults
Sorrell (2011) | Ban on using prescriber data for marketing | Struck; content- and speaker-based; "too persuasive" isn't a reason
Zauderer (1985) | Contingency-fee cost disclosure | Upheld; factual, prevents deception
Milavetz (2010) | "Debt relief agency" label | Upheld; factual, prevents deception
NIFLA (2018) | Abortion-services and unlicensed notices | Struck; not about own services, controversial; hypothetical and burdensome
CTIA (9th Cir. 2019) | Cell phone RF safety notice | Upheld; health and safety suffices

### Stretch Exercise: Graphic Cigarette Warnings

| Analysis
Issue | A 2009 federal statute requires cigarette packs and ads to carry prominent health warnings covering 50% of the front and back of packaging and 20% of ads, with FDA-developed graphic images. The Fifth Circuit rejected the manufacturers' challenge to the FDA's latest warnings (R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, 5th Cir. 2024); the Supreme Court denied cert. Imagine it took the case.
Questions | Does Zauderer or Central Hudson (or stricter review) apply? Are graphic images "purely factual and uncontroversial"? Is there a substantial interest? Is the size requirement unduly burdensome?
Analysis | For the government: the warnings concern the seller's own product, health and safety is a substantial interest (CTIA; NIFLA preserved health warnings), and smoking's health effects are factual and not genuinely controversial. For the manufacturers: graphic images may be designed to provoke emotion rather than inform, which arguably isn't "purely factual." And a warning covering half the package may "drown out" the seller's message, as the 20% soda warning did in American Beverage. The answer likely turns on whether each image is accurate and on the burden of the size requirement.

## Chapter 9: Content-Neutral Restrictions and Expressive Conduct

Two main topics: (1) time, place, and manner (TPM) regulations and (2) expressive conduct (aka symbolic speech). They overlap, so study them together. First, revisit the most important distinction in speech law: content-neutral vs. content-based vs. viewpoint-based.

Type | Examples | Standard
Content neutral (nothing to do with the message) | "No loudspeakers in the park between 10pm and 6am"; "No picketing on Main Street during rush hour"; "No leaflets on trees in the park" | Intermediate scrutiny; the government sometimes wins, sometimes loses
