7-20 Bancroft keeps a scratched laptop and uses it on a trip | Installing software after seeing the scratch risks acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c). Use after rejection: apply Johannsen. Against Bancroft: seller said send it back, and the use was avoidable if another laptop could be found. For Bancroft: seller refused to replace first and the trip was close. Outcome is fact-dependent.

XXI. Acceptance, Notice of Breach & § 2-714 Damages — §§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717 WEEK 9

RULE Acceptance, § 2-606(1): buyer accepts when, after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, it (a) signifies the goods conform or that it will keep them despite nonconformity; (b) fails to make an effective rejection; or (c) does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.

Effect of acceptance | Rule
Owes the price | § 2-607(1)
Must notify of breach within a reasonable time or be barred from any remedy | § 2-607(3)(a)
Bears the burden of proving breach | § 2-607(4). (After rejection, the burden falls on whichever party sues.)
Loses the right to reject | § 2-607(2)
Loses the right to cancel, and cover or market damages | Unless buyer revokes. An installment contract may differ: §§ 2-612(3), 2-711(1)
Gains value-difference damages + incidental and consequential | §§ 2-714, 2-715

- Losing the right to reject means buyer can't force goods back on the seller to escape a falling market.

Notice of breach

- Purposes (Aqualon v. MAC Equipment (4th Cir. 1998), quoted p. 301): (1) prevent surprise and let the seller recommend how to fix the problem; (2) let the seller investigate and prepare; (3) open the way to settlement; (4) protect against stale claims. Also lets the seller preserve rights against its own supplier (Hebron v. American Isuzu).

- Because losing all remedies is draconian, courts are lenient, but many hold that some pre-suit notice is required; filing a complaint generally isn't enough. Reasonable time is a fact question (§§ 1-205, 1-202; Golden v. Den-Mat). Content: see § 2-607 cmt. 4.

- Don't confuse: § 2-605 applies to rejected goods; § 2-607(3)(a) applies to accepted goods.

- The parties may fix a reasonable time (§§ 1-205(b), 1-302). Whether they could dispense with notice altogether is an open question in the text.

Damages for accepted goods
RULE § 2-714: (1) for any nonconforming tender (e.g., late or short), the loss resulting in the ordinary course of events, determined in any reasonable manner. (2) For breach of warranty, value as warranted − value as accepted, at the time and place of acceptance, unless special circumstances show proximate damages of a different amount. (3) Incidental and consequential damages in a proper case.

RULE Deducting from the price, § 2-717: on notifying the seller, buyer may deduct all or part of its damages from any price still due under the same contract.

- Contract price plays no part in the § 2-714(2) formula. A buyer that struck a bad bargain keeps its bad bargain, and one that struck a good bargain keeps that too.

- Repair cost is a common proxy for value difference, not the statutory test. The text asks whether cost of repair or cost of replacement better measures the lost expectancy. Where repair costs more than the drop in value, the seller argues for the smaller figure; if repair leaves the goods worth less, the buyer adds the leftover loss.

- Consequential damages carry the same four limits as in Section XVIII and can far exceed the price.

Problems
Problem | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
7-21 Baker: replacement parts promised by April 4 haven't come | Trick: nothing was accepted, so § 2-607(3)(a) doesn't apply. No notice is required for nondelivery. Still tell Supplier about the mounting loss, demand delivery, and start looking for cover, which protects consequential damages.
7-22 Notice clause for kitchen appliances | Set a specific period running from when buyer discovers or should discover the defect (e.g., 30 days), and state how to give notice. Keep it reasonable: § 1-302(b) bars manifestly unreasonable time limits, and a clause that cuts off hidden-defect claims risks §§ 2-302, 2-719. Be more generous to consumers than to restaurants.
7-23(A) (not assigned) #1 tomatoes contract $10; tender #2; at acceptance #1 = $9, #2 = $7 | ($9 − $7) × 10,000 = $20,000 to deduct. The $10 contract price isn't used.
7-23(B) (not assigned) #1 = $12, #2 = $9 | $3 × 10,000 = $30,000.
7-24(A) 500 rail cars at $20,000; repair $10,000; repaired value $19,000 | Railroad's $11,000 is right only if cars as delivered were worth $9,000: it is using repair cost as a proxy for value lost. Seller answers that § 2-714(2) measures value, not cost. If delivered value was $15,000, damages are $5,000 per car; spending $10,000 on a $5,000 problem doesn't raise the measure, unless special circumstances apply.
7-24(B) Repair $10,000; repaired value $22,000 | Railroad comes out ahead of what was promised ($22,000 vs. $20,000). Subtract the $2,000 betterment: $8,000.
7-25(A) (not assigned) | Add up: excess cost of replacement boards, cost of installing replacements, repair of sold computers, shipping, and disposal, then test each for foreseeability and proof. The future repairs of the remaining 3,000 computers raise certainty.

XXII. Revocation of Acceptance — § 2-608 WEEK 9

RULE § 2-608(1): buyer may revoke acceptance of a lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substantially impairs its value to him if he accepted it (a) on the reasonable assumption the nonconformity would be cured and it has not been seasonably cured; or (b) without discovery, where acceptance was reasonably induced by the difficulty of discovery or by the seller's assurances. § 2-608(2): within a reasonable time after buyer discovers or should have discovered the ground, and before any substantial change in the goods' condition not caused by their own defects. Not effective until buyer notifies seller.

| Rejection | Revocation
Standard | Any nonconformity (§ 2-601) | Substantial impairment of value "to him"
Compared with § 2-612 | — | § 2-612 lacks "to him"; whether that changes the test is an open question in the text
Timing | Reasonable time after tender; shorter | Reasonable time after discovery; apparently longer (cmt. 4)
Notice content | § 2-605 can bar unstated defects | No specific content required (cmt. 5)
Wrongful but effective? | Yes | No such thing. Revocation works only if it is both justified and properly notified (§ 2-709 cmt. 5)
Effect | Not an acceptance | Undoes the acceptance; not a cancellation (cmt. 1)

- After a justified, effective revocation: buyer doesn't owe the price, may cancel, and has every remedy of a buyer that rightfully rejected (§ 2-711(1)), including the same rights and duties for goods in its possession and the § 2-711(3) lien (§ 2-608(3)).

- Seller's cure after revocation is unsettled. The syllogism says yes: same rights and duties as rejection, and rejection allows cure. The answer: § 2-608(3) speaks of duties "with regard to the goods," not the seller's performance. And after § 2-608(1)(a) revocation, cure has already had its chance; a (1)(b) revocation may be different. See Lile v. Kiesel (Ind. Ct. App. 2007) (no right to cure after revocation) (cited only, n.44).

Problems
Problem 7-26 (not assigned) | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
(A) Shirts discolor; 45 of 100 bolts used | Revoke for the unused bolts. For the 45 used, the change came from the defect only if discoloration is the defect, not from cutting and sewing. Commercial units help.
(B) Motorcycle burns up | The defect caused the change, so that bar doesn't apply. Revocation mostly adds the refund; injury is consequential.
(C) Promised fuel-line repair never made | § 2-608(1)(a).
(D) Repeated leaks; roof to be sawn off | Each failed repair strengthens substantial impairment; refusing a major repair is reasonable.
(E) Assorted-color binders; replacements never come | Notably easy to see, so (1)(b) fails; (1)(a) fits.

Problem 7-27 (Steelsmith / Ballistics) | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
Was the machine accepted? | Likely yes. Two-hour test, "a little more time," then a month's use with the problem known by June 21: § 2-606(1)(a)–(c). So rejection is too late, and revocation is the question.
Can Ballistics revoke? | Yes, probably. 40 instead of 50 bullets a minute is substantial impairment to a buyer needing that rate. Acceptance was induced by difficulty of discovery: a two-hour test didn't show it, and even its engineers couldn't find the cause. July 1 notice is within a reasonable time after discovery, and the notice needs no particular content.
Must it accept repair? | Unsettled. § 2-508(1) is out: the time for performance has passed. § 2-508(2) needs reasonable grounds to think the tender acceptable. Lile says no cure after revocation; the syllogism says otherwise. If a court finds a cure right, refusing repair may be Ballistics' breach.
Use until September 1? | Reasonable and necessary under the Johannsen factors: keeps production going and mitigates. Expect an offset for value of the use.
Result | If revocation stands: Ballistics owes no balance, recovers the $125,000 down payment, and takes cover: $750,000 − $500,000 = $250,000 if Epoch's machine is a reasonable substitute and not an upgrade. It holds a § 2-711(3) lien on the machine for the money it paid. If revocation fails: it owes the $375,000 balance, less § 2-714(2) damages (machine at 50 per minute vs. 40), deducted under § 2-717.
7-28 Standard Plywood (not assigned) | Usage of trade may decide if 90 sheets per pallet conforms. 45 pallets instead of 50 is a shortfall, and inspection was wrongly refused. Selling for $80 and the 24-day delay raise acceptance and § 2-604 issues.

XXIII. Privity & Remote Sellers — § 2-318 WEEK 10

- A contract claim normally needs privity. Vertical privity: a buyer in the chain of title suing a seller further up the chain (consumer vs. manufacturer). Horizontal privity: a non-buyer outside the chain, injured by the goods. Vertical privity exists only between immediate links; a buyer who didn't buy directly from a seller is "remote."

- First ask whether the remote seller made any warranty to this buyer. Express warranty under § 2-313? Implied warranty under § 2-314? Or a warranty to the distributor or retailer that extends to the buyer?

- Article 2 barely addresses privity. § 2-318 offers three alternatives, and comment 3 leaves room for case law on the distributive chain.

§ 2-318 | Who is protected | Injury covered | Vertical privity
Alt. A (majority) | Natural persons in buyer's family or household, or guests in buyer's home | Injury in person | Silent; left to case law
Alt. B | Any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected | Injury in person | Implicitly abolished
Alt. C | Any person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected | "Injured": some states include property or economic loss | Eliminated

- A seller can't exclude § 2-318's reach, but disclaimers and remedy limits that bind the buyer bind beneficiaries too (§ 2-318 cmt. 1). Section VI has the overview of § 2-318.

MAIN CASE Hyundai Motor America, Inc. v. Goodin (Ind. 2005) — no vertical privity for a consumer's implied warranty claim Source: principal case, casebook pp. 328–337. No class slides. Facts: Sandra Goodin bought a new Hyundai Sonata from a dealer, with a 5-year/60,000-mile manufacturer warranty. Brake trouble began almost at once, and eight months of repairs didn't fix it. Her lawyer sought a refund; she sued Hyundai under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. The jury found for Hyundai on express warranty but for Goodin on the implied warranty of merchantability, awarding $3,000. The Court of Appeals reversed for lack of privity, feeling bound by a footnote in Martin Rispens. Held: Indiana doesn't require vertical privity between a consumer and a manufacturer for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, even for economic loss. The footnote was dicta. Alternative A speaks only to horizontal privity and leaves vertical privity to the courts. Privity's freedom-of-contract rationale has "eroded to the point of invisibility" for many consumer goods: goods reach consumers through intermediaries; warranties are marketing tools; consumers expect merchantability; the law spreads the cost of lemons across all buyers; and a disclaimer in the dealer's buyer's order would otherwise leave her without a remedy. The privity bar began as a limit on tort claims (Winterbottom) and was undercut by MacPherson and Henningsen. Why it matters: The modern consumer rule, but courts remain divided. Limits: it speaks to a consumer against a manufacturer, for goods subject to Magnuson-Moss. Damages are usually the § 2-714(2) value difference.

After Goodin

- Express warranty: even privity states may not require it. A manufacturer shouldn't escape its public claims because the buyer bought through a dealer (p. 337).

- Open questions when privity falls away (pp. 338–339): Can a remote buyer reject or revoke and get a refund from the manufacturer, and of which price? May it recover § 2-712 or § 2-713 damages? Must notice go to the manufacturer, or is notice to the retailer enough? Are consequential damages tested by what the manufacturer or the retailer knew? When does the limitations period start? Which state's law applies when only one has abolished privity? Does a distributor owe the same duty?

- Only sellers make implied warranties. "Seller" = one who sells or contracts to sell (§ 2-103(1)(d)), and a sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)). Auctioneers, brokers, and other agents without title almost always aren't sellers.

- Amazon: for third-party vendors' goods, courts have held Amazon isn't a seller and makes no warranty, despite listing, payment processing, storage, and shipping. The § 2-403(2) entrustment argument fails for three reasons: Amazon may never possess the goods, and the vendor's identity is disclosed; an entrustee isn't necessarily "the seller"; and Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties anyway.

Problems
Problem 7-31 (copier: Manufacturer warrants 3 years from purchase, sold June 1, 2021; Distributor disclaims all, sold Dec. 1, 2021; Retailer warrants 1 year, sold to Buyer April 1, 2022) | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
(A)(1) Privity abolished; fails Nov. 1, 2022 | Retailer: yes, on the 1-year warranty (through April 1, 2023) and on merchantability, unless disclaimed. Manufacturer: yes, on its express warranty and implied warranty if they reach Buyer. Whether a warranty on order forms Buyer never saw extends to it is a real issue. Distributor: no; its disclaimer works and it binds those below it.
(A)(2) Fails Nov. 1, 2023 | Retailer's 1-year warranty has expired. Implied warranty requires a defect at tender, and the four years hasn't run. Manufacturer's 3 years still runs on either reading of "date of purchase."
(A)(3) Fails Nov. 1, 2024 | Manufacturer: covered only if "purchase" means Buyer's purchase (through April 1, 2025), not Distributor's (ended June 1, 2024). Implied warranties remain only if the defect existed at tender and suit is timely (§ 2-725).
(B) Privity not abolished | Implied claim only against Retailer. Express claim against Manufacturer may survive, though this warranty wasn't a public statement. Retailer has no recourse past Distributor's disclaimer: the gap privity creates.
(C) Fire destroys VP's home; no injury to anyone | VP isn't the buyer, so this is horizontal. Alt. A: no. VP isn't family, household, or a guest of a corporate buyer, and wasn't injured in person. Alt. B: no; property loss only. Alt. C: yes where "injured" includes property, against Retailer (and Manufacturer, since vertical privity is gone). Distributor still protected by disclaimer. Tort remains.
7-32 Homeowner and Renovator, privity state | Make Homeowner a party in privity with the appliance seller: have Homeowner buy directly, or have Renovator buy as Homeowner's agent. Or have Renovator assign its warranty rights to Homeowner (§ 2-210), and get the seller to name Homeowner an intended beneficiary. The renovation contract alone can't bind the seller. Add Renovator's own express warranty.

XXIV. Seller's Remedies: Roadmap & When the Buyer Has the Goods — §§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702 WEEK 11

- Buyer's basic duties: accept and pay in accordance with the contract (§ 2-301).

- Walk the facts in order. Was the seller's refusal to tender justified (buyer failed to pay first, or to answer a proper demand for assurance)? Or was it a breach? Or does neither party breach, e.g., goods destroyed without fault? Is the buyer's breach excused? Are the seller's remedies limited?

- § 2-703 is an incomplete catalog. It has no "and" or "or," so it doesn't say which remedies combine (cmt. 1). The answer comes from § 1-305: no overcompensation. As with the buyer, the remedies depend on the nature of the breach and who has the goods.

Situation | Seller's remedy | Cite
Buyer accepted and won't pay | The price + incidental damages. Buyer may offset for nonconformity (§§ 2-714, 2-717) | §§ 2-709, 2-607(1)
Buyer has goods; payment device fails; or buyer took goods on credit while insolvent | Limited reclamation | §§ 2-507, 2-702(2)
Seller has the goods or they are in transit: repudiation, failure to pay before delivery, wrongful rejection, refused cure, wrongful revocation | Withhold or stop delivery; cancel; resale, market, or lost-profit damages; rarely the price | §§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705, 2-706, 2-708, 2-709
Any of these | Incidental damages, not consequential | §§ 2-710, 1-305(a)

RULE Action for the price, § 2-709(1): when buyer fails to pay the price as it becomes due, seller may recover the price, with incidental damages, of (a) goods accepted, or conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk of loss passed to buyer; and (b) goods identified to the contract if seller is unable after reasonable effort to resell them at a reasonable price, or circumstances reasonably indicate that effort would be unavailing.

- "Commercially reasonable time" limits only the lost-or-damaged goods, not accepted goods (p. 399 n.1).

- Worked example (p. 400): custom sign, $6,400; accepted; color wrong; buyer spends $1,300 reprinting brochures to match. Buyer owes $6,400, less any § 2-714 value difference and, if recoverable under § 2-715, the $1,300, deducted under § 2-717.

Getting goods back from a buyer that won't pay

- The general rule surprises people: an unpaid seller doesn't get the goods back. The principal right is the price, which is only as good as the buyer's ability to pay. Two exceptions:

- (1) Article 9 security interest. The seller who takes one may repossess peaceably or by replevin on default (§ 9-609). One sentence creates it: "seller retains a security interest in the goods sold to secure the buyer's obligations under this agreement." A clause that seller "retains title" does the same thing and no more, because title passes on delivery and the reservation is limited to a security interest (§§ 1-201(b)(35), 2-401(1), 9-109(a)(5)).

- (2) Reclamation. A restitutionary remedy, not an expectancy measure. Not self-help: if buyer doesn't return the goods voluntarily, seller must go to court.

| § 2-507 (failed payment) | § 2-702(2) (credit sale to an insolvent)
When | Cash sale: payment due on delivery; payment device fails, e.g., a check bounces. A check at delivery counts (§ 2-511 cmts. 4–6). A credit sale or post-dated check does not | Seller sold on credit and discovers buyer received the goods while insolvent (§ 1-201(b)(23))
Deadline | Reasonable time after the payment fails | Demand within 10 days after receipt, unless buyer misrepresented solvency to this seller in writing within 3 months before delivery
Other remedies | No similar limit | Successful reclamation excludes all other remedies as to those goods (§ 2-702(3)), apparently even incidental damages
Subject to | Rights of good faith purchasers, covered in Chapter 10 (not assigned) | Buyers in ordinary course and good faith purchasers (§ 2-702(3))

- Why the § 2-702(3) bar? Possibly reclamation rests on a rescission for fraud, so no expectancy remains; and the insolvent buyer's other creditors shouldn't be pushed further behind.

- Practice point: a seller on credit should take a security interest; reclamation is too narrow to rely on.

- Problem 9-1 (4,000 gallons of milk, into a vat with 5,000 others; half the vat becomes ice cream; demand June 7 for June 1 delivery): demand is within 10 days and the sale was on credit, so § 2-702(2) applies. Treat the milk as fungible: § 2-105(4) lets an undivided share of a bulk be identified. Supplier's share is 4/9. Half the vat remains (4,500 gallons), so Supplier can reclaim about 2,000 gallons. Nothing for the ice cream, which is no longer the goods sold. The casebook cites Wheeling-Pittsburgh and Charter and gives no answer; the result is worked from the statute.

XXV. When the Seller Has the Goods: Withhold, Stop, Cancel — §§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705, 2-612 WEEK 11

- Withhold = seller has the goods. Stop = a carrier or other bailee has them.

RULE Withholding: seller may withhold delivery if buyer (1) wrongfully rejects, (2) wrongfully revokes, (3) fails to make a payment due, or (4) repudiates (§ 2-703(a)). If seller discovers buyer is insolvent, it may refuse delivery except for cash, including payment for all goods already delivered under the contract (§ 2-702(1)).

RULE Stopping in transit, § 2-705(1): seller may stop delivery in a carrier's or bailee's possession when it discovers buyer's insolvency (any size of shipment). For repudiation, failure to make a payment due before delivery, or any other right to withhold or reclaim, it may stop only carload, truckload, planeload, or larger shipments. § 2-705(2): the right ends on buyer's receipt; a bailee's (non-carrier) acknowledgment to buyer that it holds for buyer; a carrier's such acknowledgment by reshipment or as a warehouse; or negotiation to buyer of a negotiable document of title.

- Three questions: (1) does seller have the right as against buyer? (2) must the carrier obey? (3) who is liable if the carrier obeys or disobeys?

- Carrier, § 2-705(3): seller must give notice enabling the carrier, by reasonable diligence, to prevent delivery. The carrier must then hold and deliver as seller directs, and seller is liable for ensuing charges or damages. If a negotiable document was issued, the carrier need not obey until the document is surrendered. A carrier with a nonnegotiable bill need not obey a stop order from anyone but the consignor.

- Stopping is limited because of the burden on carriers (cmt. 1). Related: shipping under reservation (§ 2-505), which in effect gives seller a security interest and lets it withhold the goods until paid.

RULE Cancellation, § 2-703(f): in a non-installment contract, seller may cancel on any buyer breach. No notice is required. Cancellation ends future performance and doesn't waive damages (§ 2-106(4)). Installment contracts: seller may cancel the whole only if the breach substantially impairs the value of the whole contract (§§ 2-612(3), 2-703). Short of that it may demand assurance and suspend (§ 2-609; § 2-612 cmt. 6).

Problems
Problem | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
9-2(A) Diamonds shipped F.O.B. seller; negotiable bill naming seller as consignee; buyer misses funds transfer | A parcel isn't a carload, so nonpayment alone gives no right to stop. Only insolvency would. A default to its main lender is evidence of insolvency (§ 1-201(b)(23)) but not conclusive: ask whether buyer has generally ceased paying debts or can't pay as they come due. Holding the bill in its own name also gives seller practical control (§ 2-505).
9-2(B) Must Federated obey? | § 2-705(3)(c): not until the negotiable bill is surrendered. If it delivers to buyer without the bill, it risks misdelivery liability to the holder, seller. It should hold and ask for the bill.
9-2(C) Nonnegotiable bill | § 2-705(3)(d): the carrier need not obey anyone but the consignor. Seattle Gems is the consignor, so Federated must follow § 2-705(3)(b), with seller liable for charges and damages. Rightfulness against buyer is still the question in Part A.
9-3 500 stoves in two lots; first 250 accepted; $20,000 check bounces; 250 in warehouse | Advise: (1) withhold the second lot (§ 2-703(a)). (2) Sue for the $20,000 due; a bounced check leaves the debt alive. (3) Possible § 2-507 reclamation, but only the 20% was due on delivery, so it is at best a partial cash sale, and act fast. (4) Check insolvency (§ 2-702): cash terms, and a 10-day demand if goods came on credit while insolvent. (5) Demand adequate assurance (§ 2-609) and suspend. (6) Cancel only if the breach substantially impairs the whole (§ 2-612(3)). Failure to give assurance within 30 days is repudiation, which supports cancelling and reselling the 250.

XXVI. Seller's Damages — §§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708, 2-709, 2-710 WEEK 11

- Four alternatives, all protecting the expectancy (§ 1-305), all with incidental damages: resale, market, lost profit, price. Seller can't stack resale and market.

- Worked example (pp. 408–410): $10,000 lithograph, buyer defaults. Worth $9,000: resell and get $1,000 (§ 2-706), or keep it and get $1,000 (§ 2-708(1)). Worth $11,000 or $10,000: no resale or market damages. Unlimited supply: the resale isn't a substitute, because Dealer would have made both sales, so its loss is the profit on one extra sale (§ 2-708(2)). Nobody else wants it: the price (§ 2-709), and buyer gets the print.

- Market damages are the more traditional remedy: they resemble the seller reselling to itself at market (n.11).

Measure | Formula | Key conditions | Plus / less
Resale § 2-706 | Contract − resale | Good faith; commercially reasonable in every aspect; notice | + incidental − saved
Market § 2-708(1) | Contract − market at time and place for tender | Proof of market price (§§ 2-723, 2-724) | + incidental − saved
Lost profit § 2-708(2) | Profit (including reasonable overhead) + costs reasonably incurred | § 2-708(1) inadequate; typically lost-volume sellers | + incidental
Price § 2-709 | Contract price | Accepted, or lost after risk passed, or can't be resold at a reasonable price | + incidental; hold goods for buyer

Resale — § 2-706
RULE § 2-706: where resale is in good faith and commercially reasonable, seller may recover contract price − resale price, + incidental damages, − expenses saved. Every aspect (method, manner, time, place, terms) must be commercially reasonable, and the resale must be reasonably identified as referring to the broken contract. Private sale: reasonable notification to buyer of the intent to resell (§ 2-706(3)). Public sale (auction): (1) only identified goods unless there is a recognized futures market; (2) at a usual place if available; (3) reasonable notice of time and place, except perishables; (4) goods available for inspection if not in view; (5) seller may buy.

- Resale isn't required. Seller resells because market price may be hard to prove and the resale price is known, and because sellers rarely want the goods.

- A bad resale doesn't cost seller its claim. It only loses this measure and falls back on § 2-708 (§ 2-706 cmt. 2).

- Good-faith purchaser takes free of the original buyer, even if seller botched the requirements (§ 2-706(5)). Seller keeps any profit on resale (§ 2-706(6)).

- Unidentified goods: the goods need not exist or be identified at breach (§ 2-706(2)), and § 2-704(1) lets seller identify conforming goods in its possession or control when it learned of the breach. With fungible goods, proving which sale replaced the broken contract can be hard, like a buyer proving which purchase was cover. Wisconsin Cranberry v. Groupe Alimonco (Wis. Ct. App. 2016): other sales weren't substitutes (different product, special contracts, much smaller load). Apex Oil v. Belcher (2d Cir. 1988): resale six weeks later unusable; delay unreasonable and seller had sold conforming oil the next day (cited only, n.15).

RULE Unfinished goods, § 2-704(2): seller may, in the exercise of reasonable commercial judgment to avoid loss and for effective realization, either complete manufacture and wholly identify the goods, or cease and resell for scrap or salvage, or proceed in any other reasonable manner. § 2-704(1)(b) lets it resell unfinished goods demonstrably intended for the contract.

Market — § 2-708(1)
RULE § 2-708(1): unpaid contract price − market price at the time and place for tender, + incidental damages, − expenses saved. Ignore the word "unpaid" for now: prepayments are handled separately (Section XXVII). The formulas are "strongly worded suggestions"; if one misses the expectancy, follow § 1-305.

- Seller's timing rule differs from the buyer's: time for tender, not when the party learned of the breach. The text asks why a seller treating repudiation as an immediate breach must wait for a later price.

- § 2-723(1) exception: if a repudiation case comes to trial before the time for performance, use the price when seller learned of the repudiation.

- Proof is hard for unique goods and easy for fungibles with published quotations (§ 2-724).

NOTE CASE Peace River Seed Coop. v. Proseeds Marketing (Or. 2014) — market damages after a resale Source: note case: the casebook quotes it in nn.17–18, p. 415. No class slides. Held: An aggrieved seller may claim § 2-708(1) market damages even if it resold and market damages exceed resale damages. A fixed-price contract allocates market risk, so market damages are what the parties bargained for. A seller isn't required to resell, so mitigation can't force it to use the resale price, and the UCC rejects election of remedies. Why it matters: Answers the question the text poses: resale and market are alternatives, but resale doesn't necessarily lock the seller into its resale price. Counterargument: § 1-305 forbids a recovery above the seller's real loss, and the resale shows that loss. A seller can avoid § 2-706 simply by not identifying the resale to the broken contract (n.19).

- Resale price vs. market price: the difference may reflect the passage of time (who bears that risk?) or the seller's negotiating skill. If seller recovers market damages and later resells higher, § 2-706(6) suggests no accounting.

Lost profit — § 2-708(2)
RULE § 2-708(2): if § 2-708(1) is inadequate to put seller in as good a position as performance, damages = the profit (including reasonable overhead) seller would have made, + incidental damages, + due allowance for costs reasonably incurred, and due credit for payments or proceeds of resale.

- Remedy of last resort, and implicitly available only if resale damages are also inadequate.

- Lost-volume seller: a jobber with unlimited supply is the clearest case; the breach costs it one sale, and any resale would have happened anyway.

NOTE CASE R.E. Davis Chem. Corp. v. Diasonics, Inc. (7th Cir. 1987) — who is a lost-volume seller Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, p. 418 (n.20). No class slides. Held: Capacity alone isn't enough. Ask not only whether seller could have produced the breached units on top of its actual volume, but whether it would have been profitable to do so. Under diminishing returns, at some volume the next sale stops being worthwhile, and awarding presumed lost profit would overcompensate. Why it matters: A manufacturer must show capacity and profitability. The usual test on an exam.

Lost-profit math (pp. 419–421) | Why
Profit = sale price − fixed costs − variable costs | Fixed = overhead (rent, CEO salary). Variable = rises with output (raw materials)
Statute adds overhead back: recovery = sale price − variable costs | Saves allocating overhead to one contract
Add unreimbursed reliance costs: recovery = sale price − variable costs + unreimbursed reliance | "Due allowance for costs reasonably incurred": money already spent that seller can't recover, because it gets only profit, not the price
Ignore "due credit for ... proceeds of resale" | Likely a drafting mistake. Applied literally it would almost always leave a lost-volume seller with nothing, contrary to § 1-305

- Wages and utilities can go either way: fixed if the sale was small against normal output; variable if it needed overtime. Tax treatment has little bearing.

- Direct, not consequential. A seller's lost profit comes from the breached contract itself, so foreseeability and mitigation limits generally don't apply (contrast a buyer's lost profits on resale, which are consequential).

- Lost profit is no ceiling. A buyer can't use a low or zero profit to cut market or resale damages: § 2-708(2) applies only when other measures are inadequate, not when they are higher (Trans World Metals v. Southwire (7th Cir. 1985), the leading case, n.26).

- Problem 9-8 (not assigned): lathe sold for $90,000; cost $80,000 + $2,000 parts + $1,500 preparation. Lost profit = $90,000 − $83,500 = $6,500 (the $500 overhead isn't deducted). Add unreimbursed reliance: $1,000 cancellation fee + $1,200 parts it can't reuse ($2,000 − $800) = $8,700. Market damages are zero ($90,000 market), and § 2-708(1) is inadequate if Sawtooth is lost-volume.

The price, when the seller keeps the goods

- Why the price? If seller truly can't resell, resale price is meaningless, market price may not be $0, and lost profit leaves seller stuck with its production costs. So § 2-709(1)(b) gives the contract price.

- Seller must hold the goods for buyer while suing. If resale becomes possible it may resell before collecting; net proceeds are credited. Payment of the judgment entitles buyer to any goods not resold (§ 2-709(2)).

- If seller is held not entitled to the price, it still gets § 2-708 damages (§ 2-709(3)).

NOTE CASE Foxco Indus. v. Fabric World, Inc. (5th Cir. 1979) — "unable to resell at a reasonable price" Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, pp. 423–424 (n.27). No class slides. Held: Seller of specially made spring fabric needed only reasonable efforts to resell at a reasonable price. The goods were made for a customer, were hard to sell after the spring season, and the market fell 50%. The jury could find seller acted reasonably even though it made little resale effort for months and sold part only the next season. Why it matters: Goods need not be worthless. The test is reasonable effort and a reasonable price, and market collapse and seasonality count.

Incidental damages, no consequential damages
RULE § 2-710: commercially reasonable charges, expenses, or commissions incurred in stopping delivery, in transporting and caring for the goods after breach, in connection with return or resale, or otherwise resulting from the breach. No consequential damages for sellers absent a provision: § 1-305(a), and most courts agree (Validsa v. PDVSA, n.28). So separating incidental from consequential matters. The nature of the loss counts, not its amount: incidental storage costs reached $293 million in Commonwealth Edison v. Allied Chem. (n.29).

Problems
Problem | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
9-4(A) Instructions for reselling used copiers | Decide private vs. auction. Private: send buyer notice of intent to resell. Auction: give time and place, make the machines available to inspect, use a usual place. Identify each resale to the broken contract in your records. Resell promptly in the normal channels, on normal terms, at the best reasonable price. Don't delay for a better market; keep records.
9-4(B) 100,000 gal, $5, F.O.B. Miami, 10¢ freight saved. Resold $4.75 F.O.B. Cincinnati; storage $1,000 | ($5.00 − $4.75) × 100,000 = $25,000 + $1,000 incidental − $10,000 freight saved = $16,000. The 2¢ to Cleveland is the new buyer's cost under F.O.B. Cincinnati.
9-5 $6,400 sign; $4,000 spent, $800 to finish. Salvage nets $100; or $2,000 to modify, 50% chance of $5,000 | Salvage: lost profit $1,600 + costs incurred $4,000 − $100 = $5,500 from buyer, plus $100 salvage = $5,600, the same as finishing a paid contract ($6,400 − $800). Modify: expected return 50% × $5,000 = $2,500 − $2,000 = $500, vs. $100. Better on expected value by $400 to $450, depending on salvage if unsold, so it is defensible under § 2-704(2). If the sale works, buyer owes about $2,600; if not, about $7,500. Seller's risk: if a court finds it unreasonable, it eats the $2,000. Salvage is the safe choice. Finishing for $800 makes no sense: no one else wants the sign.
9-6(A) Repudiated Feb. 15; shipment by Feb. 25; delivery by March 1. Market $4 (Feb. 15), $4.25 (Feb. 25), $4.50 (March 1). Resale March 7 at $4.75; notice given | Resale valid: $16,000 as in 9-4(B). Market: F.O.B. destination means tender at Miami on March 1: ($5.00 − $4.50) × 100,000 = $50,000 + $1,000 − $10,000 = $41,000. Under Peace River seller may take market damages despite resale; a court applying § 1-305 strictly would hold it to $16,000.
9-6(B) No notice of resale | Private sale without notice fails § 2-706(3), so § 2-708(1): $41,000. The $4.75 can still be evidence of market value, and § 2-706(6) means no accounting for the difference.
9-7(A) 10,000 gal/yr at $5 for 10 yrs; repudiated Year 6; trial August Year 9 | Years 7–9 are past due at trial: use tender-date prices. Year 10 isn't due: § 2-723(1) uses the price when seller learned of repudiation, $4.00. Per gallon, less 10¢ saved: Y7 $0.80, Y8 $0.70, Y9 $0.50, Y10 $0.90 = $2.90 × 10,000 = $29,000.
9-7(B) Trial in Year 11; Year 10 market $5.50 | § 2-723(1) doesn't apply. Y7–Y9 = $20,000. Year 10 is above contract, so no damages for that year; netting its $0.60 gain per gallon, as § 1-305 suggests, gives $14,000. Which one depends on whether the contract is treated as a whole.
9-9(A) Custom container, $3,000; cost $1,800; best offer $1,500; standard units $2,000 | Probably no action for the price: $1,500 may be a reasonable price for a customized container, so seller can resell. Resale damages: $3,000 − $1,500 = $1,500 + incidental. If $1,500 isn't reasonable, § 2-709(1)(b). The dollars are similar either way.
9-9(B) Only scrap at $500 | Yes: scrap isn't resale at a reasonable price. Recover $3,000, hold the container for buyer, and credit net proceeds if it is sold (§ 2-709(2)).
9-11(A) Pre-breach loan for general operations | Not incidental: an ordinary business cost, unrelated to the breach.
9-11(B) Pre-breach loan to finance this contract | Not incidental: incurred regardless of the breach. It is a cost of performance, which is recovered, if at all, through the price or as reliance.
9-11(C) Post-breach loan for an investment planned with the price | Consequential, so not recoverable: lost use of the money.
9-11(D) Post-breach loan to finish the machine and resell it | Strongest case: "in connection with ... resale" under § 2-710, and the finishing is authorized by § 2-704(2).

XXVII. Prepaying Buyers, Casualty & Limitations — §§ 2-718(2)–(4), 2-709(1)(a), 2-510(3), 2-725 WEEK 11

RULE Restitution to a breaching buyer, § 2-718(2)–(3): when seller justifiably withholds delivery because of buyer's breach, buyer gets back any amount by which its payments exceed (a) enforceable liquidated damages (§ 2-718(1)); or (b) with no such term, 20% of the value of its total performance or $500, whichever is smaller. Buyer's right is offset to the extent seller establishes (a) a right to damages under other Article 2 provisions and (b) benefits buyer received. Payment in goods counts at its value or resale proceeds (§ 2-718(4)).

- It works as a type of statutory liquidated damages. Sellers may keep the statutory amount without proving harm, or prove larger damages and offset them.

- Example (Problem 9-12, not assigned): $90,000 lathe, $20,000 down; market $80,000 at tender. (A) Valid $10,000 LD: return $10,000. (B) No LD: the statutory retention is $500, the smaller of that and 20%, and seller may offset damages it proves (§ 2-718(3)), such as market damages ($90,000 − $80,000) or lost profit, plus incidental damages. Compare Neri v. Retail Marine with McCann v. McSorley (cited only).

- Problem 9-13 (not assigned): after a wrongful revocation with goods returned: pick market vs. resale at the right place, add storage and freight, and subtract the $20,000 down payment. Note that buyer took and revoked, so § 2-718(2) (withheld delivery) doesn't fit neatly, but the § 1-305 result is the same.

Casualty to the goods — p. 428

- Risk of loss principles (Section IX): the party in control, the party likely to be insured, and the party in breach should bear the risk.

- If risk has passed to buyer and conforming goods are lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time, buyer owes the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)). Typical case: a shipment contract with loss in transit.

RULE § 2-510(3): if buyer repudiates or breaches as to conforming goods already identified before risk passes, seller may, to the extent of any deficiency in its effective insurance coverage, treat risk of loss as resting on buyer for a commercially reasonable time.

- Both parties can hold an insurable interest in identified goods (§ 2-501). After an unjustified revocation Article 2 is silent; presumably risk returns to seller once it takes the goods back (n.30).

- Problem 9-14 (not assigned): (A) lathes identified, buyer repudiates Oct. 28, lightning fire that night: buyer bears the loss to the extent of any insurance shortfall. (B) In a shipment contract risk passed on tender to the carrier, so transit damage is buyer's loss, and rejection and revocation fail because the goods conformed at tender. Seller gets the price, and buyer's recourse is against the carrier.

Statute of limitations — p. 430
RULE § 2-725: four years; the cause of action accrues when the breach occurs, regardless of the aggrieved party's knowledge. A warranty is breached on tender, unless it explicitly extends to future performance and discovery must await that performance. The parties may shorten the period to not less than one year, and can't extend it.

- Buyer's breach usually occurs when it fails to pay or wrongfully rejects. After repudiation the seller may wait a commercially reasonable time, and that time is uncertain, so sue within four years of the repudiation.

- Whether § 2-725 governs a secured seller's deficiency suit is split (nn.31–32).

XXVIII. Leases: Scope & Lease vs. Sale — §§ 2A-103, 1-203 WEEK 12

- Article 2A (1990) governs leases of goods and is modeled on Article 2, so the study question is where it differs, and why. The differences come from one fact: in a lease the lessor gets the goods back.

RULE Lease, § 2A-103(1)(j): a transfer of the right to possession and use of goods for a term in return for consideration. A sale, a retained security interest, and similar deals are not leases. A sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)); a lease transfers only limited rights, and the lessor keeps a residual interest.

Why the sale/lease line matters
Issue | True lease | Disguised sale (security interest)
Governing law | Article 2A | Articles 2 and 9
Tax | Lessor is tax owner, takes depreciation; rent is lessor's income and potentially deductible by lessee | Buyer is tax owner; payments not deductible as rent; seller may have gain or loss
Lessee's bankruptcy | Lessee keeps goods only by performing the lease | Buyer may keep goods paying over time the amounts due or the goods' value, whichever is less
Third parties | Lessor needs no public filing | Seller is a secured party and must perfect, typically by filing. Filing a protective financing statement is not evidence it's a sale (§ 9-505; n.3)

- Form and intent don't control. Economic substance does (§§ 1-203, 2A-102, 9-109(a)(1)).

RULE § 1-203(a): lease or security interest is decided on the facts of each case. The real question: is there a reasonable chance the lessor gets the goods back while they still have meaningful economic value? Yes = lease. No = sale with a retained security interest.

RULE § 1-203(b) bright-line test: a transaction in lease form creates a security interest if the lessee's payment obligation is for the term and not terminable by the lessee, and (1) original term ≥ remaining economic life of the goods; (2) lessee is bound to renew for the remaining economic life or is bound to become owner; (3) lessee may renew for the remaining economic life for no or nominal additional consideration; or (4) lessee may become owner for no or nominal additional consideration. If this isn't met, go back to the facts under (a).

- § 1-203(c) "not merely because": none of these alone creates a security interest: (1) the PV of rent equals or exceeds the goods' value at signing; (2) lessee takes risk of loss; (3) lessee pays taxes, insurance, fees, or maintenance; (4) lessee has an option to renew or buy; (5) a renewal option at or above predictable fair market rent; (6) a purchase option at or above predictable fair market value.

- § 1-203(d) nominal: consideration is nominal if it is less than the lessee's reasonably predictable cost of performing under the lease if the option isn't exercised. It is not nominal if the option price or rent is stated to be fair market value or rent determined when the option is performed.

- § 1-203(e): remaining economic life and predictable value are judged when the transaction is entered into.

- 99-year laptop (p. 466): a lease in form, but the goods are dead long before the term ends: a sale.

Problems
Problem 11-1 ($200,000 skid loader; construction company pays maintenance, insurance, and the entire $200,000 even if it returns early) | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
Threshold | Payment isn't terminable, so go through § 1-203(b)'s four prongs. Maintenance, insurance, and full payout alone don't make a sale (§ 1-203(c)).
(A)(1) 5 years, $3,900/mo; goods return to dealer | If five years is under the economic life, (b) isn't met. On the facts a five-year-old loader likely has real value, so it's a lease.
(A)(2) Option to buy at $5,000 | Is $5,000 nominal? Compare it with the predictable cost of returning (§ 1-203(d)) and with predictable value. If the loader should be worth far more than $5,000, exercise is near certain and it looks like a sale, but this one needs facts.
(A)(3) Option at $100 | Nominal. § 1-203(b)(4) met: sale with a security interest.
(B) 25 years, $2,000/mo; goods return | The term likely exceeds economic life, so § 1-203(b)(1): sale.
(C) Lessee may return early with no more payments | Not "non-terminable," so the bright-line test fails in every scenario. Go to the facts under (a). A low option price is still a sign of a sale, but the lessor bears real return risk, so likely a lease.

Hybrids and other law

- Hybrid leases, § 2A-102 (2022 Amendments): mirrors § 2-102(2). If the lease-of-goods aspects predominate, Article 2A applies. If not, only the provisions relating primarily to the lease-of-goods aspects apply. A consumer's cable box with cable service is an example. The goods part can be a finance lease (cmt. 6).

- Other law: Article 2A generally defers to certificate-of-title and consumer-protection law (§§ 2A-104, 2A-105; 15 U.S.C. §§ 1667–1667f; Regulation M). Magnuson-Moss and lemon laws might not apply to leases, one reason sellers structure deals as leases. No international convention governs leases of goods.

XXIX. Finance Leases — §§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407 WEEK 12

- The idea: the lessee picks the goods from a supplier; a bank or other financer buys them (Article 2 applies to that purchase) and leases them to the lessee. The goods usually go straight to the lessee. In form the financer is a lessor; in substance a lender. It wants no responsibility for quality, and the lessee looks to the supplier.

- The lease must still be a true lease under § 1-203. Because a finance lessor needs a real residual but doesn't want the goods, these leases often give the lessee a fair-market-value purchase option (n.6).

RULE Finance lease, § 2A-103(1)(g): (i) lessor doesn't select, manufacture, or supply the goods; (ii) lessor acquires the goods or the right to them in connection with the lease; and (iii) one of: (A) lessee receives a copy of the supply contract before signing; (B) lessee's approval of the supply contract is a condition of the lease's effectiveness; (C) lessee receives, before signing, an accurate and complete statement of the supplier's promises, warranties, disclaimers, and remedy limits; or (D) in a non-consumer lease, lessor informs lessee in writing of the supplier's identity and of lessee's rights to the promises and warranties.

Finance lease rule | Ordinary lease | Finance lease
Implied merchantability and fitness | Lessor makes them (§§ 2A-212, 2A-213) | Finance lessor makes neither. May give express warranties, but rarely does
Supplier's warranties | No special rule | Flow to lessee to the extent of its leasehold, subject to the supply contract's terms, disclaimers, and defenses (§ 2A-209(1))
Infringement warranty | Merchant lessor gives it (§ 2A-211(2)) | Not given
Interference warranty | Yes (§ 2A-211(1)) | Yes, for claims arising from lessor's own act or omission
Duty to pay | Lessee may deduct damages from rent (§ 2A-508(6)) | Hell or high water on acceptance if non-consumer (§ 2A-407)
Risk of loss | Stays with lessor (§ 2A-219(1)) | Passes to lessee (§ 2A-219)
Revocation | Like § 2-608 | Only for lessor's assurances, non-consumer (§§ 2A-517, 2A-516(2))

RULE Hell or high water, § 2A-407: in a non-consumer finance lease, the lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent upon acceptance of the goods. They bind assignees and third parties and aren't subject to cancellation, termination, modification, repudiation, excuse, or substitution without the consent of the party to whom the promise runs. Other law may validate an express covenant (§ 2A-407(3)), which is how consumer leases and backup clauses work.

- § 2A-209(3): a modification or rescission of the supply contract binds lessee unless supplier had notice of the finance lease; if it binds lessee, lessor assumes the old promises. § 2A-209(4): lessee keeps its own rights against supplier.

- Common-law defenses may survive: a fraudulent-inducement claim might defeat a hell-or-high-water clause (Faust Printing, n.13).

- Hybrid: if the goods aspect doesn't predominate, § 2A-407 covers only the goods portion. Allocate payments in the lease, or make the whole obligation irrevocable. Express hell-or-high-water clauses are common as backup (n.14).

Problems
Problem 11-3 (Lasting Data negotiates 30 servers with Sensational; Boston Finance edits the draft, buys, and leases to Lasting; servers fail) | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)
(A) Finance lease? | (i) Boston didn't select or supply: Lasting chose; editing the draft doesn't change that. (ii) Boston acquired the goods in connection with the lease. (iii) Lasting saw the draft, not the final contract with Boston's changes, so (A) is doubtful. Look for (B), (C), or (D). Likely yes, if one is satisfied.
(B) Sensational's warranties to Lasting | Express warranties and merchantability, flowing through § 2A-209(1). Fitness is disclaimed, and the disclaimer binds Lasting.
(C) Boston's warranties | No implied warranties (§§ 2A-212, 2A-213); no express ones on these facts. Only § 2A-211(1) interference.
(D) Supply deal is a lease, not a sale | Same result. § 2A-209 applies to a supply contract by which the lessor buys or leases goods.
(E) Lasting must buy at the end | Bound to become owner + non-terminable: § 1-203(b)(2) makes it a sale with a security interest. Article 2A and § 2A-209 drop out. Boston is a seller: implied merchantability only if it is a merchant in such goods; disclaim under § 2-316. Lasting's claim against Sensational now hits vertical privity (Section XXIII).
11-4(A) Effect of § 2A-407 | If Lasting accepted, it must keep paying Boston despite the defects, and pursue Sensational. If it validly rejected before accepting, § 2A-407 isn't triggered.
11-4(B) Drafting for Boston | An express hell-or-high-water clause (§ 2A-407(3)) as backup; a signed acceptance certificate; waiver of setoff and defenses against the lessor and assignees; a disclaimer of all warranties; assignment of supplier warranties to lessee; default remedies. See Wells Fargo v. B.C.B.U. (cited only).

XXX. Lease Formation & Terms — Article 2A Parts 1–2 WEEK 12

Formation

- Same as Article 2 (§§ 2A-103(1)(k)–(l), 2A-204 to 2A-206), with no analog to § 2-206(1)(b) (prompt-shipment orders), to § 2-207 (battle of the forms), or to the CISG. Why: lessees rarely send orders, and leases are negotiated rather than exchanged on forms.

Statute of frauds — § 2A-201 vs. § 2-201 (Problem 11-2)
Point | § 2-201 | § 2A-201 | Why (worked from the text)
Threshold | Price of $500 or more | Total payments of $1,000 or more, excluding option payments | Higher dollar figure; rent is spread over time
What the record must show | A contract for sale and quantity | A lease contract, a description of the goods, and the lease term | No gap filler for term, which is the core of a lease
Merchant confirmation | § 2-201(2) exception | None | Such lease transactions were thought to be few (cmt.)
Specially made goods | Yes | Yes, "manufactured or obtained," fitting a lessor who buys goods for lessee | Finance leases and lessors acquiring goods
Part performance | Goods accepted or payment made and accepted | Only goods received and accepted | A lessee pays only some rent, not a full price, which isn't a sufficient substitute for a memorandum (cmt.)
Admission | Yes | Yes | Same
Term when an exception applies | n/a | § 2A-201(5): the term in a signed record, the admitted term, or a reasonable lease term | Needed because a term is essential

- 2022 Amendments: a signed record replaces a signed writing. UETA reaches the same result elsewhere. Satisfying the statute doesn't prove a lease exists.

Unconscionability

- §§ 2A-108(1), (3) repeat § 2-302. Consumer leases add relief for procedural unconscionability: unconscionable conduct inducing the contract or in collecting a claim, with no need for substantive unconscionability (§ 2A-108(2)), and attorney's fees for a consumer lessee who prevails (§ 2A-108(4)).

- Consumer lease, § 2A-103(1)(e): a lessor regularly in the business of leasing or selling makes a lease to an individual primarily for personal, family, or household purposes [states may set a dollar cap].

Terms and gap fillers

- Same concepts of agreement, course of performance, course of dealing, usage of trade, and good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304). The casebook still cites § 2A-207, but the 2026 statutes show that section deleted, with its rule now in § 1-303.

- Few gap fillers. Nothing like §§ 2-304, 2-305, 2-306, 2-307, 2-308, 2-309, 2-310, 2-311, 2-503, 2-504, 2-505. Leases tend to be more complete, and no near-universal default exists. The common law fills gaps (§ 1-103).

- Consumer leases: limits on choice of law and forum (§ 2A-106), which don't reach arbitration.

Warranties

- Express (§ 2A-210), merchantability (§ 2A-212), fitness (§ 2A-213): same as Article 2, except a finance lessor gives no implied warranties.

- Disclaimers: § 2A-214 tracks § 2-316, except that a merchantability disclaimer must also be in writing and conspicuous. It also has an express rule for disclaiming the interference and infringement warranties (§ 2A-214(4)).

- Third parties: § 2A-216 tracks § 2-318, separate from § 2A-209.

- Title analog: § 2A-211(1) warranty against interference: no claim arising from the lessor's act or omission will interfere with the leasehold. Compare § 2-312.

Remedy limits, parol evidence, modification
Topic | Article 2 | Article 2A
Unconscionable limitation | Implicit | Express: not enforceable (§ 2A-503(2))
Liquidating consequential damages | Limit expressly allowed (§ 2-719(3)); liquidation probably allowed (§ 2-718(1)) | Expressly may be liquidated or limited (§ 2A-503(3))
Liquidated damages test | Reasonable in light of anticipated or actual harm, difficulty of proof, inconvenience of other remedy (§ 2-718(1)) | Amount or formula reasonable in light of the then anticipated harm only (§ 2A-504(1))
Parol evidence | § 2-202 | § 2A-202, almost identical
Modification | § 2-209 | § 2A-208: same, but no analog to § 2-209(3); courts resolve oral modifications case by case

XXXI. Lease Performance — Risk of Loss, Excuse & Transfers WEEK 13

- Insecurity and repudiation: §§ 2A-401 to 2A-403 follow §§ 2-609 to 2-611.

Risk of loss
RULE § 2A-219: in an ordinary lease, risk stays with the lessor. In a finance lease, risk passes to the lessee, at the time agreed or, if none, (a) on delivery to the carrier, or tender at the named destination; (b) on the bailee's acknowledgment of the lessee's right to possession; (c) otherwise on the lessee's receipt if the lessor, or in a finance lease the supplier, is a merchant; if not, on tender. Parties often shift the risk to the lessee by agreement.

- Why different from sales? Both parties hold property rights for the whole term, so the question isn't when risk passes but who carries it during the lease.

- Default, § 2A-220: a nonconforming tender leaves risk on lessor or supplier until cure or acceptance. A rightful revocation lets lessee treat risk as lessor's from the start, to the extent of any insurance shortfall. If lessee repudiates or defaults as to conforming identified goods, lessor or supplier may put risk on lessee for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of its insurance shortfall.

- Insurable interest: lessee on identification (§§ 2A-217, 2A-218(1)–(2)). Lessor keeps one until lessee has exercised a purchase option and risk of loss has passed (§ 2A-218(3)). Parties may agree who insures and who takes proceeds (§ 2A-218(5)).

Excuse

- § 2A-221 tracks § 2-613, § 2A-404 tracks § 2-614, §§ 2A-405, 2A-406 track §§ 2-615, 2-616.

- Finance-lease twist: a non-consumer finance lessee that takes damaged goods, or accepts part of a quota, pays full rent, consistent with § 2A-407.

Assignment and delegation — § 2A-303

- Lessor's assignment of the right to payment, with or without the residual, is an Article 9 transaction. Anti-assignment clauses generally don't stop the transfer or create a default (§§ 2A-303(2), 9-406(d), 9-407).

- Lessee's transfer of possession: if the lease makes it a default, lessor has default remedies (§ 2A-303(4)(a)). If it merely prohibits it, the transfer is effective unless damages would be inadequate (§ 2A-303(4)(b)).

- Delegation doesn't release the rent duty (§ 2A-303(6); compare § 2-210(1)).

XXXII. Lessor's Default & Lessee's Remedies — §§ 2A-508 to 2A-522 WEEK 13

- Default comes from the agreement and Article 2A (§ 2A-501). Lessee's remedies are in § 2A-508, and the parties may add others. No general duty to notify of default, with exceptions (§ 2A-502).

Lessee's position | Remedy | Compare Article 2
Goods not delivered | Specific performance or replevin (§ 2A-521) | § 2-716. Standard largely the same
Prepaid, identified goods | Recover if lessor insolvent within 10 days after first payment (§ 2A-522) | § 2-502(1)(b). No consumer prepayment analog to § 2-502(1)(a)
Cancel | Non-installment: any default (§§ 2A-508(1)(a), 2A-505). Installment: substantial impairment of the whole (§ 2A-510(2)) | §§ 2-711, 2-612(3)
Recover rent and security paid | Only so much as is just under the circumstances (§ 2A-508(1)(b)), since lessee may have had use of the goods (cmt. 2) | § 2-711(1) refunds the price paid
Cover by substantially similar lease | PV of new rent for the comparable period − PV of old rent + incidental + consequential − saved (§ 2A-518(2)) | § 2-712
Cover by purchase, or by a dissimilar lease, or no cover | Market rent: PV of market rent − PV of original rent, as of default, for the remaining term + incidental + consequential − saved (§§ 2A-518(3), 2A-519(1)) | § 2-713. Place for tender, or arrival after rejection (§ 2A-519(2))
Accepted goods | Loss in the ordinary course; for warranty, PV of the difference in the value of the use of goods as accepted and as warranted (§ 2A-519(3)–(4)) | § 2-714
Deducting from rent | Yes, except finance leases under § 2A-407 (§ 2A-508(6)) | § 2-717

- A purchase can't be measured as cover. Unlike a buyer, a lessee who buys replacements falls to the market-rent formula. And "substantially similar" is hard to meet given negotiated terms (§ 2A-518 cmts. 3–7).

- Market rent proof: § 2A-507.

Nonconforming tender — same model as Article 2

- Reject: non-installment: perfect tender (§ 2A-509(1)). Installment: substantial impairment of the installment and no cure or assurance of cure (§ 2A-510). Within a reasonable time, with seasonable notice (§ 2A-509(2)). Failure to state defects may waive them (§ 2A-514).

- Cure: same as § 2-508 (§ 2A-513). Care of goods: §§ 2A-511, 2A-512. Lien for prepayments (§ 2A-508(5)). A purchaser from these sales takes free of lessor's or supplier's claims.

- Acceptance: failing to reject, or signifying conformity or that lessee will keep the goods (§ 2A-515). Lessee has inspection rights, though no section parallels § 2-513. Acceptance means rent is owed and rejection is gone (§ 2A-516(1)–(2)).

- Notice after acceptance: notify lessor and the supplier, if any, or be barred against the party not notified (§ 2A-516(3)(a)). Lessee bears the burden of showing default (§ 2A-516(3)(c)).

RULE Revocation, § 2A-517: like § 2-608: substantial impairment + (a) reasonable assumption of cure or (b) acceptance induced by lessor's assurances or difficulty of discovery. Also, except in a non-consumer finance lease, lessee may revoke if lessor defaults under the lease in a way that substantially impairs the goods' value (§ 2A-517(2)), and on other defaults if the agreement says so. Finance lease: the assumption-of-cure and difficulty-of-discovery grounds are gone: only lessor's assurances remain, and acceptance with knowledge bars revocation (§ 2A-516(2)). That keeps § 2A-407 working. A consumer finance lessee may also use § 2A-517(2). Timing and duties track § 2-608.

- After revocation: cover or market rent + incidental + consequential − saved.

- Limitations, § 2A-506: four years, reducible by contract to one, and unlike § 2-725 not barred from being extended (cmt.). Accrual is more liberal than § 2-725: when the default is or should have been discovered, or when it occurs, whichever is later. Tolling is left to other law.

- Problem 11-5, worked from the text, not the professor's answer (Boston leases 30 servers to Lasting; purchase agreement sent for approval; 20 installed, 5 fail; 10 never delivered): likely a finance lease ((iii)(A) or (B)). Against Boston: no warranties. For 15 working and 5 failed installed units, if accepted, rent is due under § 2A-407, and revocation only if Boston gave assurances. For the 10 undelivered there is no acceptance, so § 2A-407 doesn't apply; Lasting can refuse rent on them and, if the deal is an installment lease, cancel if the whole is substantially impaired. Against Sensational: warranty and delivery promises through § 2A-209(1): damages for the 5, and for nondelivery of the 10, with consequential damages for customer problems unless excluded. Notify both Boston and Sensational (§ 2A-516(3)(a)). Cover, because that also limits consequential loss.

XXXIII. Lessee's Default & Lessor's Remedies — §§ 2A-523 to 2A-532 WEEK 13

- Lessor's main aim is usually to recover the goods and then damages. The residual interest gives it a much stronger claim to the goods than a seller has, but no duty to take them. Remedies are in § 2A-523, and the agreement may add others.

Lessor's measure | Formula | Compare Article 2
Substantially similar new lease (§ 2A-527(2)) | Accrued unpaid rent at start of new term + (PV remaining old rent − PV comparable new rent) + incidental − saved | § 2-706
Market rent (§ 2A-528(1)): dissimilar lease, sale, or no disposition | Accrued unpaid rent + (PV remaining rent − PV market rent at the place where goods are located, same term) + incidental − saved | § 2-708(1)
Lost profit (§ 2A-528(2)) | PV of profit incl. reasonable overhead + incidental + costs reasonably incurred, credit for disposition proceeds, with lessor keeping its residual | § 2-708(2)
Rent (§ 2A-529) | Accrued unpaid rent at judgment + PV of remaining rent + incidental − saved | § 2-709

- No consequential damages for lessors, as with sellers. Incidental damages: § 2A-530.

- Rent is available for goods accepted and not repossessed, for conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk passed, or for identified goods lessor can't dispose of at a reasonable price (§ 2A-529(1)). Lessor must hold the goods for lessee for the remaining term, but may dispose of them before collecting the judgment, and that disposition then runs through § 2A-527 or § 2A-528 (§ 2A-529(2)–(3)).

- Tender back cuts off rent. Article 2 lets a seller recover the price of accepted goods. Article 2A rejects that: if lessee tenders the goods back, lessor is limited to the damages it would have had, because it holds a residual and will re-let or sell anyway (§ 2A-529 cmt. 1). A lost-volume lessor can still reach full rent through § 2A-528(2) (cmt. 2, five backhoes never all rented).

- Residual: lessor may also recover for loss of or damage to its residual interest caused by the default, e.g., goods returned in worse condition than the lease requires (§ 2A-532).

- No notice of disposition is required from a lessor, unlike § 2-706(3). But if the "lease" may be a disguised sale, give notice anyway: § 2-706(3) and § 9-611 could apply (n.16).

- Before delivery: lessor may withhold, on default or discovering insolvency (§ 2A-525), or stop in transit (§ 2A-526, parallel to § 2-705), and may cancel, subject to substantial impairment for installment leases (§§ 2A-523(1), 2A-510(2)). Unfinished goods: § 2A-524, parallel to § 2-704.

- Wrongful rejection or revocation where lessor takes goods back: same damages as repudiation (§ 2A-523(1)).

RULE Repossession, § 2A-525(2)–(3): after default lessor may take possession, without judicial process if it can be done without breach of the peace, or by action. It may require lessee to assemble the goods if the lease says so, and may render business goods unusable. Borrowed from § 9-609: no violence or substantial risk of it; trespass is allowed; no breaking and entering, particularly of a home.

- Prepaying lessee, § 2A-504(3)–(4): if lessor justifiably withholds or stops delivery, lessee gets back payments above enforceable liquidated damages or, absent that, 20% of the then PV of total rent for the balance of the term (in a consumer lease, the lesser of that or $500), subject to offset for proven damages and benefits received. Compare § 2-718(2): sales use the lesser of 20% or $500 for every buyer.

- Risk after default, limitations: §§ 2A-220(2), 2A-506, as in Sections XXXI and XXXII.

Problems
Problem | Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's; PV ignored)
11-6 Lathes leased for $80,000 over 3 years; $20,000 down; delivered, accepted, returned a week later at lessee's unjustified demand; market rent Nov. 8: $60,000 Chicago, $55,000 Phoenix; 2-year re-lease in Denver for $50,000 | Two-year lease isn't substantially similar to three-year, so § 2A-527(3) sends it to § 2A-528(1). Goods are in Phoenix, so use $55,000: $80,000 − $55,000 = $25,000. Incidental: storage (about 60 days × $100 = $6,000) + $1,500 freight = $7,500. Total $32,500, less $20,000 already paid = about $12,500, plus any rent accrued for the week of use. Counting the $20,000 as rent paid gives the same result ($60,000 − $55,000 + $7,500).
11-7 On default: repossess, all past rent, all future rent, 5% late fee on missed payments, 12% interest on all amounts | Past rent is fine. Future rent + repossession = double recovery: lessor gets the money and the goods. Not reasonable under § 2A-504(1), so it fails and Article 2A's remedies apply (§ 2A-504(2)). Revise with a formula, which § 2A-504(1) allows if reasonable in light of then anticipated harm: past-due rent + PV of future rent + estimated residual, − net proceeds of re-leasing or sale. The § 2A-504 comment calls that formula common. Limit the late fee and 12% interest to overdue sums, not unaccrued rent.

XXXIV. Property Rights in Leased Goods — §§ 2A-304 to 2A-308 WEEK 13

- Starting point: a transferor gives only what it has. Lessee can transfer the leasehold, and lessor the residual (§ 2A-303). These rules are the exceptions. The text is deliberately brief: know which rule fits. Fixtures, accessions, and titled goods are excluded (n.18).

Transfer | Result
Person with voidable title leases to a good-faith lessee for value (§ 2A-304(1)) | Lessee takes free of the original seller's rights. Analog to § 2-403(1)
Lessor leases twice for overlapping terms (§ 2A-304(1)) | First in time: second lessee takes subject to the first lease, unless (1) lessor is disposing after breach of the first lease (§ 2A-527(4)), or (2) first lessee entrusted goods back and the second is a lessee in ordinary course (§ 2A-304(2))
Owner entrusts to a merchant, who leases in ordinary course (§ 2A-307(2); § 2A-304 cmt. 3) | Lessee in ordinary course is protected, but owner keeps the residual: it loses the goods only for the term. Analog to § 2-403(2)
Lessee with a voidable leasehold (§ 2A-305(1)) | Can transfer a good leasehold to a good-faith sublessee or buyer. Doesn't cut off lessor's residual
Merchant lessee sells or subleases in ordinary course (§ 2A-305(2)) | Buyer or lessee in ordinary course takes free of lessor. Eliminates the residual
Lessee disposes after lessor's breach (§§ 2A-511, 2A-512) | Purchaser takes free of lessor's interest (§ 2A-511(4))

Creditors
Creditor | Result
Lessor's creditor with a possessory statutory lien for services or materials | Lessee takes subject to it, whenever it arose (§ 2A-306), unless the lien law says otherwise
Lessor's creditor whose lien arose before the lease | Lessee takes subject to it (§ 2A-307(2)–(3)), unless it's an Article 9 security interest and lessee qualifies as a lessee in ordinary course (§ 9-321(c)) or gave value and took possession without knowledge while it was unperfected (§ 9-317(c))
Lessor's creditor whose lien arose after the lease | Subject to lessee's rights, except a statutory lien or a fraudulent transfer (§ 2A-308)
Lessee's creditors | Don't beat lessor's rights (§ 2A-307(1)), except a § 2A-306 possessory lien

XXXV. Week 14 Review: Final Exam Checklists WEEK 14

- Final format (syllabus): 180 minutes in three parts: 60 minutes of closed-book multiple choice, a 30-minute closed-book short bar essay, and 90 minutes of short answers with a physical statutory supplement and a 5-single-page outline. Worth 70% of the grade. It covers lectures, slides, handouts, readings, and class discussion. The syllabus lists an asynchronous review lecture for Week 14; no Week 15 appears on it.

Remedies side by side
Issue | Buyer (Art. 2) | Seller (Art. 2) | Lease (Art. 2A)
Roadmap | § 2-711 | § 2-703 | §§ 2A-508, 2A-523
Substitute transaction | Cover § 2-712: cost − contract | Resale § 2-706: contract − resale | New similar lease: PV of rent difference §§ 2A-518, 2A-527
Market | § 2-713: when buyer learned of breach, place for tender | § 2-708(1): time and place for tender | PV of market rent §§ 2A-519, 2A-528
Get the goods or money | §§ 2-502, 2-716 | Price § 2-709 | §§ 2A-521, 2A-522; rent § 2A-529
Consequential | Yes § 2-715(2) | No | Lessee yes, lessor no
Incidental | § 2-715(1) | § 2-710 | §§ 2A-520(1), 2A-530
Limitations | 4 yrs, accrues on breach § 2-725 | Same | 4 yrs, discovery rule § 2A-506
Liquidated damages | Anticipated or actual harm | Same | Then anticipated harm only

Buyer's remedy decision steps

- (1) Did seller breach? Is that excused? Are remedies limited? (2) Who has the goods? (3) Goods not delivered or repudiated: get them (§§ 2-502, 2-716), or cancel and take refund + cover or market + § 2-715. (4) Delivered: was it accepted? Check § 2-606. (5) Not accepted: was rejection rightful (§ 2-601 or § 2-612) and effective (§ 2-602; § 2-605)? Can seller cure (§ 2-508)? (6) Accepted: notice under § 2-607(3)(a), then § 2-714 and § 2-717, or revoke under § 2-608. (7) Add § 2-715, subtract expenses saved, and test against § 1-305.

Seller's remedy decision steps

- (1) Did buyer breach? Excused? Limited? (2) Buyer has the goods: price (§ 2-709), or reclamation (§§ 2-507, 2-702), or Article 9. (3) Seller or carrier has them: withhold or stop (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705); cancel. (4) Pick a measure: resale properly done? Market provable? Lost-volume with capacity and profitability? Can't resell? (5) Add § 2-710; never consequential. (6) Subtract expenses saved. (7) Account for prepayments under § 2-718(2)–(3).

Lease spot-check

- (1) Is it a true lease (§ 1-203)? (2) Is it a finance lease (§ 2A-103(1)(g))? (3) Consumer lease? (4) If finance and non-consumer: did lessee accept (§ 2A-407)? (5) Who bears risk (§ 2A-219)? (6) Apply the PV formulas, and watch which Article 2A difference the facts are built around.

TIP Traps to rehearse. Formula direction (cover − contract, contract − resale). A purchase that isn't a reasonable substitute isn't cover, so § 2-713 applies. § 2-607(3)(a) applies only to accepted goods. No "wrongful but effective" revocation exists. A seller gets no consequential damages. Nonpayment alone doesn't stop a parcel in transit. A retained-title clause is only a security interest. A $100 option on a non-terminable lease is a sale. A lessee's purchase can't serve as cover damages.
